articles.summary: Houthi attacks threaten Saudi oil infrastructure and Crown Prince's economic vision - Qatar shock  bankingnews.gr
articles.full_text:
Mohammed bin Salman's vision for a Saudi Arabia that would spearhead the global economy, attracting billions in investments and turning the desert into a symbol of luxury, technology, and power, is now confronting the harsh reality of war. Houthi missiles and drones threaten the heart of the Saudi kingdom, oil infrastructure is being transformed into targets, and Riyadh's grand ambitions are tested on the battlefield. Indicative, moreover, is the assessment that Saudi Arabia cannot defend its entire airspace and that many of its energy infrastructure facilities and installations are... vulnerable. Behind the renewed flare-up in Yemen emerges a sequence of strategic missteps: the rupture with the United Arab Emirates, the underestimation of the Houthis' military strength, and above all, the overestimation of Donald Trump's willingness to defend Washington's most important Arab ally. The result is a dangerous geopolitical stalemate: the Saudi crown prince, who sought to distance his country from regional conflicts to build its economic future, now risks seeing that future dictated by a war he believed he could leave behind.
Deep crisis
Mohammed bin Salman, crown prince of Saudi Arabia, aspired to transform his country into an international hub for investment and tourism, as well as a host for the world's largest sporting events. Today, however, unmanned aerial vehicles and missiles launched from Yemen are striking Saudi cities, dragging the country ever deeper into a regional crisis from which the crown prince hoped to remain aloof. The civil war in Yemen reignited this summer and escalated last month, ending a period of several years of relative calm. Over the past 11 years, Saudi Arabia has attempted, through both military and diplomatic means, to contain conflicts on its southern border. It initially fought against the Houthis, subsequently pursued peace negotiations with them, and restored diplomatic relations with Tehran.
Miscalculations
However, according to experts, a series of erroneous calculations left Riyadh vulnerable to a new cycle of conflict. Late last year, Saudi Arabia terminated its long-standing partnership with the United Arab Emirates due to disagreements arising from Abu Dhabi's support for a rival armed force in Yemen. Concurrently, Riyadh overestimated Donald Trump's willingness to offer support to Saudi Arabia. These developments occur during a period when multi-directional attacks on oil infrastructure have disrupted Saudi exports, led to the cancellation or postponement of major projects, and exerted significant pressure on Mohammed bin Salman's economic plans. According to Saudi officials, Houthi attacks against several of the country's airports this week resulted in the deaths of at least 13 people, including a Saudi pilot. Michael Ratney, former United States ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told CNN: "All they wanted was to keep the conflict as far away from Saudi Arabia as possible and prevent the Houthis from disrupting the country's transformation plans. Now, however, they find themselves at the center of the crisis."
The hasty withdrawal of the United Arab Emirates
Saudi Arabia's airstrike last year against a shipment of military vehicles sent by the United Arab Emirates to support the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council shattered the two countries' decade-long alliance. Following the departure of Emirati forces, Saudi Arabia was forced to face the consequences of the crisis alone. According to a southern Yemeni official, the UAE's withdrawal created a vacuum in the command of forces that had operated for years under Abu Dhabi's guidance. He underscored that the transfer of responsibilities to Saudi Arabia was not carried out smoothly and that Riyadh failed to ensure the same level of coordination and command.
Inadequate preparation against the Houthis
Eight weeks after the UAE's withdrawal, the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran broke out. These developments plunged the region into a broader crisis, exposing Saudi Arabia to Iranian attacks as well. In July, Iran dispatched a civil aircraft to transport a Houthi delegation. Saudi Arabia, seeking to prevent the aircraft from landing at Sanaa airport, which is controlled by the Houthis, launched an attack against the airport. In response, the Houthis announced the termination of the ceasefire, decided to impose a naval blockade on Saudi vessels, and initiated a rapid military operation along the Yemeni coast. Subsequently, Houthi attacks against Saudi oil installations and pipelines disrupted crude oil transport and caused prices to rise. Saudi forces responded by carrying out hundreds of airstrikes. Ahmed Nagi, senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, stated that Saudi Arabia was unprepared for the Houthi offensive and had failed to secure necessary coordination with allied forces in Yemen. He added that the Houthis' advance has undermined the morale of Riyadh's allies, while the organization's advanced weapon systems now threaten more Saudi cities.
Donald Trump: An unpredictable ally
According to experts, over-reliance on American support constituted yet another miscalculation by Saudi Arabia. Despite signing a new defense agreement with Washington, Riyadh remains anxious over diminishing American commitment regarding its security. According to CNN, Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice with Donald Trump last month, asking him to launch strikes against the Houthis. However, the American president refused to intervene. Instead, Washington conducted negotiations with the Houthis in Oman, aiming to preserve the ceasefire it had previously concluded with the organization. Michael Ratney assesses that the Saudi military structured its forces based on cooperation with the United States and was not designed to independently conduct offensive operations of this nature. According to him, the unpredictable character of Donald Trump's decisions has reinforced the sense in Riyadh that it stands alone against threats. In response, Saudi Arabia has broadened cooperation with Egypt, France, Britain, Turkey, and Pakistan. Concurrently, more than 100 American military advisors have been deployed to Saudi Arabia with a mandate to provide intelligence and assist in target identification.
A regional solution remains distant
Experts warn that external support and initial military successes by Yemeni government forces are insufficient on their own to bring the war to an end. Disagreements among armed factions, as well as the absence of a clear plan for Yemen's political future, continue to pose significant obstacles. According to analysts, as long as the war between the United States and Iran continues, Tehran will retain a strong incentive to leverage the Houthis' military capabilities to exert pressure on Saudi Arabia. A diplomatic settlement between Persian Gulf states and Iran or, alternatively, an escalation of military strikes against the Houthis rank among potential scenarios for the upcoming period. However, none of these guarantees an end to the war in Yemen in the immediate future. Saudi Arabia is now compelled to seek a difficult and inevitably imperfect exit from the crisis, which casts doubt upon both Mohammed bin Salman's regional ambitions and his economic plans.
The message of the Emir of Qatar
The Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, underscored that attacks against liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities have severely impacted the country's production capacity and inflicted immediate consequences on its economy. Concurrently, he warned that "henceforth we must not operate as we operated prior to this crisis." This message is expected to be received with utmost seriousness by both members of the Shura Council and the heads of state institutions. As he noted, the state budget for coming years will be influenced by the events of the past year.
The Emir delivered a clear message, both directly and indirectly: Qatar intends to pivot more toward economic sectors unrelated to hydrocarbons. He specifically referenced tourism and hospitality, the real estate market, the further development of the private sector and other commercial activities, as well as the enhancement of agriculture, domestic stability, and food security. From his speech, it became evident that he recognizes how the war, which has now reached the doorstep of Arab nations, has generated severe economic repercussions for Qatar. He urged greater fiscal prudence in managing state expenditures while maintaining an optimistic tone and expressing strong conviction that the country possesses the resilience required to overcome the crisis.
Diplomacy as a primary choice
Addressing the attacks launched against the country by Iran, the Emir characterized them as a blatant violation of national sovereignty and the principles of good neighborliness. As he emphasized, despite the ongoing war, the country must remain stable and prepared, utilizing the capabilities of its security mechanisms to confront and surmount crises. He also expressed gratitude toward Qatar's security forces and armed forces.
The emir reiterated that the country remains committed to negotiations without implying it will make concessions on national security matters. In doing so, he reaffirmed the enduring guideline of Qatar's foreign policy: priority given to security, while simultaneously maintaining the capability and will to negotiate with all involved parties. He underscored that diplomacy consistently represents a preferable choice over conflict. However, he warned that ongoing attacks against Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries demonstrate that aggression remains a grave problem demanding a collective response. He reiterated, in fact, the principle that an attack against any GCC nation constitutes an attack against all.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of spurring on Yemen's Houthis
articles.summary: Iran continues to arm and train Yemen's Houthi rebels, while actively encouraging the group's ongoing conflict with the kingdom, a Saudi Foreign Ministry official said Thursday. "I...
articles.full_text:
Iran continues to arm and train Yemen's Houthi rebels, while actively encouraging the group's ongoing conflict with the kingdom, a Saudi Foreign Ministry official said Thursday.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of U.N. Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the ministry, said during a virtual briefing with reporters.
He later added: "We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran."
Krimly also revealed that the country reached out to the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting escalates between the two sides, but the group refused to meet in Oman.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused. This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago," he said.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say - AP News
articles.summary: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco’s headquarters, officials say  AP NewsSaudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage in Houthi attack, sources say  ReutersAramco HQ Hit as Houthis Widen Attacks on Saudi Arabia  Bloomberg.comHouthi missile hits Aramco building after Saudi-led coalition strike on Yemen fuel depot  BBC‘Things are about to get worse,’ ex-U.S. energy official warns after attack on Saudi oil giant  MS NOW
articles.full_text:
CAIRO (AP) — Iran-backed Houthi rebels hit the headquarters of the Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco in an overnight strike, two regional officials said Wednesday, damaging the offices of the firm’s chief executive and other top officials.
The strike, in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dhahran, was the latest demonstration of the Houthis’ ability to attack high-profile targets.
There were no casualties in the attack, which the officials said damaged the building’s top three floors. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to discuss the matter with the media.
The Houthis had warned earlier they were targeting Dhahran with a ballistic missile. Late Wednesday evening, Houthi-run broadcaster al-Masirah reported strikes on the capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. The Saudi coalition has not commented on the strikes.
The sight of smoke rising from some of Saudi Arabia’s most sensitive facilities in recent days has rattled the region and global markets while increasing questions for U.S. President Donald Trump, who has said he’s evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis in the latest front in the Iran war.
The Saudi energy ministry reported a “limited fire” at the Aramco building Tuesday night. Aramco didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
On Wednesday, Saudi civil defense authorities in the capital, Riyadh, said debris from an intercepted strike had left one person injured. The state-run SPA news agency published images showing a damaged building and a vehicle with a large cylindrical object, seemingly part of a missile, lodged in its hood.
The Saudi-led coalition said that it had intercepted two Houthi drones, four cruise missiles and one ballistic missile targeting Riyadh, a ballistic missile targeting Dhahran and a cruise missile targeting Al-Kharj, a key military and industrial city. Alerts for incoming missiles were also sounded around Riyadh, though details weren’t immediately clear.
Rebels call the strikes retaliation for ones at home
The Houthis called the attacks retaliation for “treacherous Saudi aggression” against Sanaa, the rebel-held Yemeni capital, and other areas, as the kingdom backs the forces of neighboring Yemen’s internationally recognized government in a major military offensive launched a week and a half ago. The rebel-run Health Ministry reported two dead in attacks in Yemen on Tuesday and blamed the Saudis.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been targeted multiple times in the past week with strikes that have killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300 others, greatly affecting aviation across the kingdom.
The Houthis, hardened by years of civil war, have emerged as Iran’s most effective armed proxy of the moment, but experts say they also have their own agenda. Either way, they are applying increasing pressure on a key U.S. ally.
Casualties surge along Yemen’s front lines
There has been an “unprecedented surge” in combat casualties along Yemen’s front lines, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross, particularly in the city of Marib, along the Red Sea coast and the besieged city of Taiz, where the World Food Program says it can no longer reach more than 600,000 people who depend on aid.
Main roads leading into Yemen’s third-largest city have been closed amid rebel attacks, with regular clashes on the outskirts and overnight bombardment.
Residents are increasingly worried about dwindling supplies of fuel and food.
A Taiz resident, who spoke on condition of anonymity fearing the Houthis could seize the city, said that long lines now form outside shops, and public transportation has become increasingly scarce because of fuel shortages. The sound of loud explosions keeps her awake at night, she said in a telephone interview, adding that downtown Taiz hasn’t been shelled.
On Wednesday, schools in Taiz were ordered closed for a month.
Houthi official describes diplomatic outreach for a ceasefire
A senior Houthi official told The Associated Press that regional and international powers have reached out in an effort to stop the attacks on Saudi Arabia as part of a ceasefire deal.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, said that Oman has tried to get both sides back to the negotiating table, and Russia and China also tried via Iran.
“We’re welcoming any mediation that leads to an end of the war and the blockade between Sanaa and Riyadh,” he said. “We’re ready for a comprehensive end of the war and the blockade from both sides, not just a temporary ceasefire.”
The rebels continued to warn of attacks on both airports and oil facilities. More than 3,000 flights scheduled to depart from airports across Saudi Arabia have been canceled or listed as not operating in the past week, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors
The escalation has highlighted Saudi Arabia’s struggle to intercept Houthi missiles and drones. The kingdom has pressed allies like the United States for more military support. Regional officials say Saudi Arabia, the world’s top purchaser of U.S. weapons, is running low on interceptors.
The Saudis are trying to stop daily attacks across a territory about three times the size of Texas. Experts say intercepting all of the missiles and drones is impossible. The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of reaching targets well over 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away, with some warheads capable of changing direction midflight.
The Saudi-led coalition is also striking oil targets. Earlier Wednesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said that two people were killed in an airstrike on Tuesday on an oil facility near the Ras Isa port in Hodeida province. The coalition attacked another oil facility in Sanaa.
The targeting of fuel storage facilities in Houthi-controlled areas marks a new phase, said Ahmed Nagi, senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, a think tank. He said that in a war of attrition, the rebels could risk losing much of their military capacity.
“The Houthis are betting on pressure, while the Saudis are betting on time,” Nagi said.
The fighting has revived Yemen’s civil war after four years of relative calm.
“There’s a huge fear,” said one Sanaa resident, Umm Shadi, after the Saudi-led strikes there on Tuesday, adding that people are largely staying home.
UN detainee released by rebels
A United Nations staff member detained by the rebels has been released, the U.N. special envoy for Yemen said Wednesday. Sami al-Kalabi, who was detained in June 2024, has been freed, Hans Grundberg said. Last week, the World Food Program announced the release of one of its employees.
The Houthis continue to hold 71 U.N. workers arbitrarily detained over the past few years. Aid workers are often held for months without charges, accused of being spies for the West or Israel, claims their families deny.
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Marzouk al-Jaberi in Taiz, Yemen, Fatma Khaled in Cairo, and Sarah El Deeb in Beirut contributed to this report.

articles.title: Houthis vow to ramp up Saudi attacks after hitting oil giant's HQ
articles.summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Wednesday to continue attacking Saudi Arabian airports and oil facilities, day after a strike that sources said heavily damaged the Saudi Aramco headqua...
articles.full_text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Wednesday to continue attacking Saudi Arabian airports and oil facilities, day after a strike that sources said heavily damaged the Saudi Aramco headquarters.
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the U.S.-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Tuesday night's attack on Saudi Aramco's base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh Wednesday and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The Saudi government media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.
In their statement Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
In a broad threat, they urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations center for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Riyadh's international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
Authorities have closed the airport until Oct. 17 and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.
The U.N. brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Red Cross said Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.
The U.N. World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.
"WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children," WFP said in a statement.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy - The Conversation
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.
As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.
Houthi narratives
The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.
It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.
What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.
A belated return to war
When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.
But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.
Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.
Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.
An earlier airport bombing
During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.
The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.
From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.
After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.
The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.
Saudi’s Houthi blowback
The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.
Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.
These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.
With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.
This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.
It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.
Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia vetoes Israeli push to join fight against Houthis: Report - Türkiye Today
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia vetoes Israeli push to join fight against Houthis: Report  Türkiye Today
articles.full_text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has rejected an Israeli push, made through U.S. mediation, to join the military campaign against Yemen's Houthis, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported, citing a diplomatic source.
"The Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been trying to convince Saudi Arabia to allow Israel to intervene, but the crown prince is not interested in Israeli assistance because joining with Israel would not look good to Saudi public opinion," the source said.
Israeli military intervention in Yemen is "out of bounds" because of the crown prince's veto, the source told the Israeli media outlet.
The report highlights Tel Aviv's hope of using the Yemen war to move toward normalization with Saudi Arabia, as Houthi strikes on the kingdom, including deadly attacks on Riyadh's airport, escalate.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
Saudi Arabia does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, and its official position is that normalization is possible only after real progress toward a Palestinian state.
Trump has repeatedly promoted Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, and the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham had worked to make Saudi-Israeli normalization the basis of a post-Iran war regional order.
After Saturday's attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, Netanyahu wrote on X: "I strongly condemn the horrific terror attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which claimed the lives of 12 innocent people and injured hundreds more. On behalf of the people of Israel, I express our deepest condolences to the families of the murdered and wishes for a full recovery to the wounded."
The Houthis advanced along Yemen’s western coast in early September, seizing the port city of Mocha and several Red Sea islands and gaining control of the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Yemeni government forces have since launched a broad counteroffensive with Saudi-led air support, as the fight against the Houthis widens.

articles.title: Israel plans inland ports to counter Houthi threats and Iranian tensions - Ynetnews
articles.summary: Israel plans inland ports to counter Houthi threats and Iranian tensions  Ynetnews
articles.full_text:
Amid concerns over the development of alternative trade routes in the region, including a trade corridor being promoted by Turkey and Syria, the Israel Ports Company is stepping up pressure on the government to advance Israeli participation in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). In the coming weeks, the company is expected to submit a first-of-its-kind strategic plan for the establishment of inland ports in Israel for government approval, it was announced Thursday morning at the Mare Med conference in Tel Aviv.
The plan is intended to serve as the first practical step toward implementing the initiative in Israel by creating physical and logistical links between seaports, the railway network and logistics centers. The move aims to establish Israel as a major trade hub between Asia and Europe and shift the project from the planning stage to implementation.
The announcement came during a special international forum convened by the Israel Ports Company, attended by senior officials and professionals from Israel, the United States, Greece, the European Union and Jordan, alongside representatives of shipping companies, the operator of Haifa Port, Ashdod Port and Israel Shipyards.
Participants agreed to establish a permanent international professional forum and working groups to ensure ongoing coordination. The groups will meet every two months to address regulatory and operational obstacles.
The growing urgency surrounding the corridor stems from continued turmoil in global shipping and maritime trade. Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea have severely disrupted commercial shipping toward the Suez Canal, forcing many shipping companies to reroute container vessels around Africa.
At the same time, regional tensions with Iran and persistent concerns over threats to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz have driven up maritime insurance costs and intensified the search for alternative routes.
As global supply chains face frequent disruptions, IMEC is increasingly viewed as a strategic asset. The proposed corridor would combine a maritime route from India to the Persian Gulf with a rail and logistics network running through Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel's seaports, which would serve as gateways to ports in Greece and the rest of Europe.
For both the Israeli and global economies, the project promises to reduce costly shipping times and establish a stable trade artery that does not depend on vulnerable maritime chokepoints.
"IMEC is a historic opportunity to turn Israel into a major trade hub, and the question is not whether the project will be implemented, but when," Israel Ports Company CEO Pinchas Tsruya said Thursday morning.
"The vision is clear and the need is critical, but competition over global trade routes is intensifying, and the window of opportunity will not remain open forever."
Tsruya added that "establishing the international working groups is an important practical step toward realizing the vision and securing Israel's place in the trade routes of the future."
Israel Ports Company Chairman Hezi Halavia said at the conference that "the IMEC corridor is not merely a logistics route, but a strategic bridge connecting the Middle East and Europe. A strong and resilient supply chain is built on docks, railways and logistical, technological and human infrastructure."
Halavia also emphasized that "establishing Israel's position within IMEC is not only an economic initiative, but a central component of the country's strategic standing in the region and its national resilience for decades to come."
Government officials say implementing the project will require faster procedures than those currently used for developing national infrastructure.
"Israel has an enormous opportunity to become a hub connecting economies, promoting growth and generating a long-term strategic advantage. Government-owned companies are responsible for a significant portion of the infrastructure that will enable the project to be implemented, and the Government Companies Authority will work to advance it," said Roi Kahlon, director of the Government Companies Authority.
Kahlon added that "the government must create the conditions, powers and tools that will allow companies to operate quickly, flexibly and efficiently."
A central focus of Thursday morning's discussions was the maritime and overland connection to Greece, which is seeking to establish its ports, particularly Piraeus and Thessaloniki, as the corridor's gateway to the European Union.
"Israel is an essential partner in the region. Its geographic location, port infrastructure and technological capabilities make an important contribution to developing reliable and modern connectivity," said Greece's ambassador to Israel, Maya Solomou.
"Greece is ready to cooperate with Israel and all the other partners to help realize the corridor's full potential," the ambassador added.

articles.title: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry - The Guardian
articles.summary: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry  The GuardianJudge Blocks Trump Administration’s Sanctions on 2 Groups Aiding the I.C.C.  The New York TimesU.S. Sanctions ICC in a Bid to Avoid “Criminal Liability”: War Crimes Prosecutor Reed Brody  Democracy Now!Nobel Peace Prize Winner Pillay Criticizes U.S. After Trump Rages About Losing Award  ForbesU.S. Court Blocks Enforcement of ICC Sanctions against Groups Advocating f...
articles.full_text:
A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza.
In a 30-page order issued on Tuesday, Jesse M Furman, a judge at the US district court for the southern district of New York, granted a preliminary injunction to the two groups, Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag).
The two organizations sued the Trump administration this summer, challenging an executive order issued in February 2025 that imposed sanctions against the ICC.
The order warned the US government would “impose tangible and significant consequences” on people involved in investigations that Washington said threatened the national security of the US or its allies, including Israel.
The order came after the ICC issued arrest warrants for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant, accusing them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Both men have rejected accusations against them, and the US government also opposed the court’s decision to issue the warrants.
In his opinion, Furman noted that last year two law professors brought a separate lawsuit challenging the 2025 executive order, and that the court had held that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny”.
Furman said that this lawsuit brought by Dawn and Taag – groups he described as “American advocacy organizations” – raised a “substantially similar challenge”. He wrote that the groups were challenging the 2025 order on “both statutory and constitutional grounds, re-upping many of the arguments made in the earlier cases”.
Dawn and Taag are rights groups that had worked to gather information for the ICC as it investigated allegations of war crimes against Palestinians.
“The court concludes that the 2025 order likely violates plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constitutes a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and cannot survive strict scrutiny,” Furman wrote.
However, the judge stopped short of declaring the executive order “facially unconstitutional” and rejected the groups’ request to “enjoin the president and to enter a ‘universal’ injunction barring enforcement of the 2025 order against anyone”.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on the ruling.
A spokesperson for the US state department said in a statement to the Guardian that “we do not comment on pending litigation” but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”
Joseph Pace, a lawyer for Dawn and Taag, described Tuesday’s decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”.
And in a statement, Omar Shakir, Dawn’s executive director, said: “Today, a US federal court has put the brakes in a major way on the Trump administration’s efforts to shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.”
Dawn also said that it would “immediately resume” its advocacy with the ICC “to prosecute Israeli and American perpetrators of grave crimes”.
The ruling comes just days after the US imposed financial sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition, Houthis issue tit-for-tat evac orders for oil sites
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Houthis and the rebels issued tit-for-tat evacuation orders Tuesday for civilians and workers to evacuate oil facilities. The coalition supporting...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Houthis and the rebels issued tit-for-tat evacuation orders Tuesday for civilians and workers to evacuate oil facilities.
The coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government called on civilians to evacuate an oil facility in the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, ahead of a planned military operation.
In a statement, coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki urged civilians to leave the Yemen Petroleum Co.'s Al-Sabaha central station for their safety.
"The Joint Forces Command of the Coalition requests that civilians evacuate the site of the Yemen Petroleum Company, the al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa ... for their own safety," al-Maliki wrote on X, attaching a map of the location on the city's outskirts.
The evacuation warning came shortly after al-Maliki announced on X that the coalition will issue an alert to civilians ahead of "precision operation."
The announcement comes amid renewed tensions between the coalition and Yemen's Houthi group.
Later Tuesday, in an apparent response to the coalition statement, Yemen's Houthis warned civilians and employees to evacuate areas near Saudi Aramco facilities.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all employees and citizens near any facility belonging to Aramco oil to evacuate it and move away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
Yemen's Houthis warned Tuesday all employees and civilians near facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco to evacuate and stay away from the sites.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group considers any Aramco oil facility a "legitimate target" for its forces.
The tit-for-tat warning comes amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?  Al JazeeraSaudi Arabia says it thwarted a missile strike on Medina, and other Middle East developments  AP NewsOil price hikes, Saudi-Houthi strikes carry on amid Trump's midterm pause on Iran war  Fox NewsHouthis deny targeting holy city of Medina after Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missile  France 24Saudi Arabia intercepts three missiles as capital’s international airport remains cl...
articles.full_text:
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.

articles.title: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: Why Trump is likely to join Saudi war against Houthis  Responsible StatecraftSaudi Airlines Rush to Save Scores of Planes From a War Zone  WSJWhy advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia  NBC NewsHow are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?  ReutersHouthis emerge as global threat beyond Iran control amid Saudi strikes, former envoy warns  Fox News
articles.full_text:
For myriad obvious reasons, President Donald Trump has so far resisted calls from Saudi Arabia to assist in its fight with the Houthis, even as the militant group has been striking — literally — at the heart of the Kingdom's oil and tourism industries all week.
First, the U.S. can hardly afford another front in its current Middle East war. We know Pentagon munitions stockpiles are depleted, and our main asset in the region, the U.S. Navy, is stretched thin trying to manage its blockade against Iran and helping to shuttle non-sanctioned shipping through the Strait of Hormuz (which is not going as well as the White House was boasting a week ago).
Second, politically, Trump cannot afford to launch another war ahead of the midterms, especially if it is not guaranteed to be successful. His first escalation against the Houthis in 2025 failed, and he was forced to call a ceasefire. The Yemeni resistance group, also known as Ansar Allah, has only gotten stronger since.
But the pressure is on, and Annelle Sheline, research fellow at the Quincy Institute's Middle East program, says it is likely that Trump will be forced to get involved sooner than later.
"Part of why we've seen the Trump administration not give in to Mohammed bin Salman's request to engage directly in attacking Ansar Allah inside Yemen is because the Saudis kicked the Emiratis out of Yemen last January," Sheline told me this morning, referring to remnants of the two nation's joint involvement in the first Yemeni Civil War. "The U.S. is very closely aligned with the UAE, which is obviously very closely aligned with Israel, and so there's a sense from the administration that the Saudis made their bed and now they need to lie in it. But that does imply that after Trump feels that the Saudis have been made to suffer, then he will get involved more directly."
Perhaps even more urgently, MBS may put on the table all of its investments in the U.S. that Trump had only been touting a year ago when he did his much ballyhooed tour of the Middle East. At the time he said he got pledges for $1 trillion from the region, including $600 billion from Saudi Arabia. A $142 billion arms deal was also announced at the time.
Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy.
"Just given how we know things work in Washington, there are obviously many pressures from the U.S. defense industry, from the fact that Mohammed bin Salman has personally enriched Trump and his family, including Jared Kushner's various expensive endeavors," Sheline said, noting the president's son-in-law's close investment ties with the Kingdom, which are now a focus of a congressional investigation.
The Quincy Institute's Trita Parsi said he agrees the U.S. lurch in defense of Saudi Arabia is likely, but thinks Trump may wait for the midterms. "I think Trump's preference is for it to happen afterwards. But it may not be under his control if he sees further escalation by Iran or the Houthis," he told me.
It is definitely on the president's mind. In response to a direct question of involvement on Sunday he said, "We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
On Tuesday he said the Houthis were "behaving very badly" and blamed the group for attacking Saudi Arabia to purposely spike oil prices before the midterms. Meanwhile, CBS News speculated that the death of an American in the Houthi attack on Riyadh's biggest airport on Saturday, "may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate."

articles.title: Iraq gains new Red Sea trade link as Saudi NEOM port advances Gulf logistics corridor - Iraqi News
articles.summary: Iraq gains new Red Sea trade link as Saudi NEOM port advances Gulf logistics corridor  Iraqi News
articles.full_text:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq may get access to new trade routes connecting Europe, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia after an agreement between Port of NEOM and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics to investigate integrated cargo services linking the Red Sea with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations and Iraq.
The planned logistical corridor comes as the region’s war worsens and shipping via the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, making other trade routes more important for Iraq and other Gulf nations.
Under a memorandum of understanding, the two corporations will look into methods to optimize the flow of products along the Europe-Egypt-Saudi Arabia-GCC-Iraq corridor by integrating marine shipping with land transport, customs clearing, storage, and cross-border distribution.
The Port of NEOM, situated in Saudi Arabia’s northwestern Red Sea area, is being developed as a logistics hub linking international shipping lines to domestic markets.
The cooperation would use the port’s marine links and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics’ regional transport network to provide companies with better coordinated cargo services between ports and ultimate destinations.
For Iraq, the corridor might offer an extra route for imports and commercial cargo coming from Europe and other foreign markets, thus decreasing dependence on regular Gulf shipping routes.
The effort also emphasizes Saudi Arabia’s expanding importance in linking Iraq to regional and worldwide supply chains, especially as corporations seek alternatives to sea routes vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions.
The company seek to study combined customer service, market growth, and logistical solutions for various sorts of cargo.
The arrangement is still exploratory, with no precise investment value, implementation timeline, or verified cargo quantities stated.
While the planned corridor has the potential to increase Iraq’s economic relations with Saudi Arabia and other GCC nations, its actual effects will be determined by the development of cross-border transportation services, customs procedures, and business demand.

articles.title: As Houthis approach Yemen's Taiz locals flee fear of another siege
articles.summary: As Iran-backed Houthi rebels push to capture the strategic city of Taiz in Yemen's 12-year civil war, fear gripped the locals with many deciding to flee. Weam Abdullah and her fami...
articles.full_text:
As Iran-backed Houthi rebels push to capture the strategic city of Taiz in Yemen's 12-year civil war, fear gripped the locals with many deciding to flee.
Weam Abdullah and her family are among the war-displaced population leaving Yemen’s third largest city. They had survived a yearslong siege by the rebels earlier in their country’s civil war and they didn’t want to endure that again.
They made it out just in time. Shortly after Abdullah, her husband and two young children left, the rebels captured a key town on Oct. 4, largely encircling Taiz and cutting off most supply routes from government-held areas.
"We already feel dead, there was already despair” in the city, Abdullah told The Associated Press by phone from a province farther south. "We feel as if we are cursed. Everyone is conspiring against us even though we’re not affiliated with any party or politics.”
The assault follows a lightning offensive last month in which the rebels seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, strengthening their ability to attack Saudi oil shipping and plunging global energy prices further into turmoil.
The advance has triggered fear among Taiz's more than 1 million residents, who live in the rugged mountains of southwestern Yemen. On a recent day, crowds mobbed groceries in the city center to buy up food and other essentials, fearing they will soon run out. Diesel fuel and cooking gas supplies are running low, residents said.
Some residents are collecting cardboard and wood to burn for cooking, while merchants are raising food and water prices, said Shaif al-Gabiri, a child protection consultant at the Civic Center for Advocacy and Support, a local nonprofit group.
"If the siege continues, then these stocks will run out," he said.
Explosions from fighting between Houthis and pro-government forces echo from the surrounding mountains. Some strikes have hit the city itself, reminding residents of an ordeal they hoped might be over.
Taiz has been on the front line of Yemen’s civil war since 2014 when Houthi rebels seized the north and much of the country’s west, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia later entered the war at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government, which had been forced to flee south.
A strategic gateway to the south, Taiz is also one of Yemen’s most important historical and cultural centers. It once served as the capital of several Islamic dynasties and a major center of religious learning.
Al-Qahira Castle, a monumental fortress more than 800 years old, overlooks the city from a hill. To the south rises Mount Sabir, more than 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) high, its slopes carved into agricultural terraces.
For much of the war, Houthi forces surrounded most of Taiz and blocked its main roads. Bombardments regularly struck the city center, power cuts were frequent, and residents struggled to find food.
The only routes to government-held areas were steep, winding mountain back roads. Bringing in supplies or getting people to hospitals in the southern port city of Aden took hours.
Taiz was "a jungle" at the time, Abdullah said. If people didn’t die "from artillery, then they would die from the siege, malnourished because of lack of food," she said. After nightfall, "many streets were deserted and looked scary."
A truce reached in 2022 eased fighting across Yemen and brought some life back to Taiz. Many who had fled returned, and homes were rebuilt. But prices remained high, and residents struggled to get by, Abdullah said. Houthi forces still controlled areas north, east and west of the city and charged "customs” duties on supplies passing through.
The truce ended in August when the Houthis launched a new assault. Last month, they seized the Red Sea coast, capturing the port city of Mocha and several strategic islands. They then began advancing around Taiz.
Abdullah said her family feared a new siege would be worse than the last. Her children were afraid to go outside to play.
"This is why we left," she said. "The situation was terrible, you couldn’t get essentials, and there’s a shortage in everything ... There is no diesel to work water pumps."
As they fled Taiz, they saw government reinforcements heading toward the city and heard explosions and gunfire, she said. They passed through Turbah, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Taiz, before reaching the government-controlled province of Lahj.
Days later, the Houthis captured Turbah, encircling Taiz and a pocket of government-held territory.
As well as the main roads out of Taiz, some of the alternative mountain routes used in the past are now closed, causing "some confusion and panic," according to Abdelrahman al-Qaliaa, director of the Taiz branch of the Industry and Trade Ministry.
He urged residents crowding stores to only buy what they immediately needed to prevent shortages.
Pro-government forces are fighting Houthis in the mountains southwest of Taiz, trying to break the rebels' hold.
Ahmed Abdel-Jaber said shelling near his house in a mountain village wounded his 7-year-old grandson in his stomach. The boy was taken to a hospital in Taiz.
Abdel-Jaber moved his family of nine to another village farther from the fighting. "If we decide it’s unsafe there, we’ll flee to another area," he told the AP by phone.
Growing numbers of government soldiers, women and children wounded in the fighting have been brought to hospitals in Taiz.
"Hospitals could run out of diesel at any point," said Dr. Fahd Nazary of the Taiz provincial health office. Delivering medical supplies has also become more difficult, he said. "This is a huge catastrophe."
Al-Gabiri, the child protection consultant in Taiz, described fears that the fighting could worsen.
"Here I am sitting in a coffee shop," al-Gabiri said, "knowing that at any moment a shell could fall on me or an explosive could come from any direction, hitting any house and any street."

articles.title: Houthi strikes mark the end of Saudi Arabia's Yemen 'containment strategy' - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Houthi strikes mark the end of Saudi Arabia's Yemen 'containment strategy'  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia’s bid to “contain” the Houthis in Yemen while doubling down on economic growth at home is collapsing, posing one of the most serious tests for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since he rose to power, according to analysts and diplomats.
A decade ago, the crown prince led the kingdom into a war aimed at ousting the Houthis from power. The conflict turned into a quagmire for Saudi Arabia, sapping its resources and sparking widespread backlash due to its devastating bombing campaign. In the end, Saudi Arabia cut its losses and maintained an uneasy truce with the Houthis since 2022.
“This is the collapse of Saudi Arabia’s containment strategy,” Rob Geist Pinfold, an international security expert at King's College London, told Middle East Eye.
“The way Saudi Arabia approached the Houthis in the last few years was not dissimilar to how Israel treated Hamas in Gaza before 7 October [2023]. The Saudis felt they had the Houthis where they needed them. They weren’t at the stage to reach a political solution, but they felt they had disincentivised them from escalating again.”
The conflict erupted again after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Houthi officials from landing. MEE reported that Iranian, Syrian and Hezbollah military advisors were on board along with weapons systems.
The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping as a result, and launched a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast last month, which the kingdom and its Yemeni allies have struggled to counter.
'Literally striking'
Unlike the last time a full-scale war raged in Yemen, Saudi Arabia now has more to lose from a widening of the conflict, and the Houthis have become more sophisticated adversaries, experts say.
Saudi Arabia faced Houthi missile and drone attacks during the last round of fighting, but they were nowhere near as precise as this time.
In the last week alone, the Houthis struck Riyadh’s international airport three days in a row. A strike on Saturday killed at least 13 people and injured 300. The group’s targeting capabilities were underscored again on Tuesday when they hit the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state oil giant, Aramco, in the eastern city of Dhahran.
The strikes have caused some to question the capabilities of Saudi Arabia’s military.
The kingdom is a major buyer of American weaponry, including Patriot and Thaad air defence systems. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the kingdom spends 6.5 percent of its GDP on military gear, one of the highest ratios in the world.
“It’s quite striking, literally, that the Houthis can hit, at will, these incredibly important facilities in Saudi Arabia and the Saudis can’t defend them,” Gregory Gause, an expert on the Gulf at the Middle East Institute, told MEE.
“They clearly have much better missiles and targeting technology than they did before,” he said.
A western defence official in Riyadh told MEE that Saudi Arabia is absorbing the vast majority of missiles and drones fired at it, saying the number is likely in the low 90 percent range. But the Houthis are more skilled at penetrating the kingdom’s air defences.
“The Houthis are a lot more effective than Iran was back in February. They learned from earlier this year,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It is a combination of innovation, rapid speed and the latest intelligence,” the official said.
The Houthis honed their targeting skills after 7 October 2023, attacking vessels in the Red Sea in what they claimed was solidarity with besieged Palestinians in Gaza. A four-year ceasefire gave the group time to entrench itself in Yemen’s rugged northwestern mountains. They have also received more assistance from Iran and even Russia, MEE has reported.
The gap between aerial offence and defence is not new. Israel is constantly innovating its air defences, and the war between Ukraine and Russia has become a testing ground for new military hardware.
The problem for Saudi Arabia is that it has more to lose from a return to fighting this time.
Who has more to lose?
Saudi Arabia is more connected to the global economy than it was in 2015. It is loath to issue a prolonged closure of Riyadh airport because it is hosting a flagship investment conference at the end of the month, experts say.
The costs of a new escalation are also high. Saudi Arabia generally avoided the worst of Iran’s retaliation against the US and Israel’s attack in February. The kingdom benefited from selling oil at higher prices, as it flexed its stability. That advantage proved fragile.
Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was temporarily disabled in a strike last month that the kingdom blamed on Iran-aligned militias in Iraq.
'A Houthi strike on Riyadh airport is so much more damaging to the Saudis than a Saudi strike on Sanaa airport is to the Houthis'
- Gregory Gause, Middle East Institute
The kingdom’s economy is already under strain. Saudi Arabia expects its economy to shrink by 3.6 percent this year and has already had to scale back megaprojects that formed part of its Vision 2030 economic plan. A wider war could put more pressure on the kingdom's purse.
“The Saudis can bomb the Houthis as many times as they want, but it doesn’t hurt them because they aren’t interested in creating a modern economy,” Gause said.
“A Houthi strike on Riyadh airport is so much more damaging to the Saudis than a Saudi strike on Sanaa airport is to the Houthis,” he added.
The one advantage Saudi Arabia has this time is that it has a bit more sympathy abroad.
Diplomats and analysts say Saudi Arabia has generally responded with restraint to the Houthi attacks. Video footage from the Houthis' Saturday strike on Riyadh airport showed Umrah pilgrims absorbing the blast, sparking widespread condemnation against the group.
'Is Saudi Arabia too dovish?'
“The Saudis have upped their game when it comes to more precise air raids,” Bader al-Saif, an expert at Kuwait University, told MEE.
The kingdom wants to keep the international community on its side, experts say, especially for wider strategic reasons. Early this month, it activated the Mecca Pact - a joint defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey. Islamabad has already sent military aid to Saudi Arabia, and Turkey is expected to.
The US, Saudi Arabia's closest ally, has so far refused to become publicly involved in the conflict, although it has sent defensive support and intelligence, experts say.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman hosted Democratic Senator Chris Murphy earlier this month in Riyadh. Murphy was one of the sharpest critics of the war in Yemen before the 2022 ceasefire. Notably, he did not call for Saudi Arabia to stand down this time.
Saif, at Kuwait University, said Saudi Arabia may be acting with too much restraint.
“I think you need to flex some muscle. Being dovish when you are being attacked is not quite wise,” he said. “The Houthis need to be pushed to the negotiating table, and that means forcing changes on the ground,” he said.
Because Saudi Arabia is loath to deploy its own ground forces into Yemen, it needs to rely on its local allies.
The kingdom is the biggest backer of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, but those forces are deeply fractured.
'Melted away, showed up unarmed'
The Yemeni government announced earlier this month a full-scale military offensive whose aim is to retake all the territory held by the Houthis since 2014. But a western official in the Gulf tracking the offensive said he was “disappointed” in their performance.
“The capabilities of Yemeni government forces have been hyped up in recent months, but they have been pretty defective,” the official said. “One force showed up to fight without food and water. Other units have just melted away, leaving the flanks exposed.”
The most effective fighters against the Houthis are Yemeni factions aligned with the UAE. Saudi Arabia clashed with the Gulf neighbour over its support for these forces' secessionist ambitions, complicating efforts to create a cohesive military.
Last month, Saudi Arabia hosted UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed in a bid to mend fences with its neighbour. But on Tuesday, the exiled head of Yemen’s secessionist movement, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, appeared in a video with a map of the former southern Yemeni state behind him.
Yemen was divided in two from 1967 to 1990, with southern Yemen as an independent Marxist state.
Although Zubaidi called for mobilisation against the Houthis, he also called on the global community to recognise the constitutional declaration of a southern Yemeni state.
"His appearance was unnecessary and revealed the underlying Saudi-Emirati divergence despite Abu Dhabi’s messaging of solidarity. His statement was not one of cohesion,” Ibrahim Jalal, an independent expert on Yemen and the Arab Gulf, told MEE.
Still, Jalal said that the counter-offensive was still in its early days and Saudi Arabia could do more to empower its local allies. “The Houthis can go further up the escalation ladder than Saudi Arabia,” he said. “So Saudi Arabia needs to arm the government of Yemen in a way that is more enabling.”
Gause, at the Middle East Institute, told MEE that Saudi Arabia is unlikely to change the realities on the ground in Yemen without broader regional deconfliction.
The Houthis have internal motivations for their offensive, but experts say their calculations can’t be separated from the stalled ceasefire between Iran and the US.
“The only practical path the Saudis have right now is pushing the US to have an end to the conflict with Iran. The only way the Houthis get restrained here is if the Iranians tell them to. That can only come from a US-Iran political deal,” he said.

Why It Matters
Congress faces renewed questions about how to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons as disputes over international sanctions, limited access for nuclear inspectors, and uncertainty surrounding diplomatic negotiations complicate efforts to monitor and restrict Tehran's nuclear activities. 
United Nations sanctions on Iran were reimposed on Sept. 27, 2025, after France, Germany, and the United Kingdom invoked a mechanism under the 2015 nuclear agreement, according to a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. The move restored restrictions on Iran's nuclear and missile programs, extended U.N. Security Council oversight and raised questions about international enforcement, nuclear inspections and the Trump administration's Iran policy.
The Big Picture
The Congressional Research Service published a report titled "Iran's Nuclear Program and 2025 UN Sanctions Reimposition," examining the sanctions' restoration and the status of Iran's nuclear program. The sanctions were lifted under the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 multilateral agreement that limited Iran's nuclear activities in exchange for sanctions relief. President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the agreement in 2018 and subsequently pursued renewed economic pressure on Tehran.
France, Germany and the United Kingdom invoked the agreement's sanctions "snapback" mechanism on Aug. 28, 2025. The Security Council did not adopt a resolution to maintain sanctions relief, so sanctions were restored on Sept. 27. The restored measures include restrictions on arms transfers, ballistic missile technology and nuclear-related trade. The reimposition also indefinitely extended Security Council consideration of Iran's nuclear program, which otherwise was scheduled to conclude on Oct. 18, 2025.
However, China, Iran and Russia disputed the European countries' authority to invoke snapback, arguing that they had failed to fulfill their own commitments and exhaust the agreement's dispute-resolution procedures.
The CRS report also raises concerns about monitoring Iran's nuclear activities. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) withdrew inspectors following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. The extent of damage to Iran's enrichment capabilities remains unclear because inspectors have been unable to access affected facilities.
A June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran called for negotiations over Iran's nuclear program and U.S. and U.N. sanctions, although it did not specify future international inspection arrangements.
The Bottom Line
Congress faces questions about sanctions enforcement, nuclear monitoring and the relationship between U.S. law and the restored U.N. restrictions. Lawmakers may also examine how the administration's diplomatic negotiations address Iran's nuclear capabilities, international inspections and competing interpretations of the Security Council's authority.
