In early May 2018 U.S. Pres. Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the JCPOA, vociferously criticizing aspects of the deal that he believed were insufficient. Furthermore, he said that the United States would resume economic sanctions on Iran in November. Trump’s announcement was sharply criticized by Iran and was met with dismay and disappointment by the other countries party to the agreement. Iran and the remaining signatories stated that they planned to abide by the original pact, although it remained to be seen how that would be accomplished in the face of the U.S. withdrawal. Moreover, because U.S. sanctions included penalties for countries and businesses that continued to trade with Iran, the resumption of sanctions undermined the ability of those signatories to carry out their end of the deal.
For the next several months, the international community prepared for sanctions primarily by cutting oil imports or withdrawing businesses from Iran. The EU, moreover, began developing a special purpose entity (SPE) to avoid penalties for European companies doing business with Iran, known as the India, Italy, Greece, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Turkey to continue importing oil from Iran for six months. Those exemptions expired in May 2019.
The effects of the renewed sanctions were devastating to Iran’s economy. The economic improvement after the JCPOA had not trickled down to most Iranians in the first place, and, with reversal of the benefits of the nuclear agreement, GDP shrank and inflation soared to its highest rate since the mid-1990s. In the spring of 2019, when the country suffered catastrophic flooding that affected nearly 2,000 communities across the country, Iran asserted that the sanctions strangled the inflow of financial aid from abroad.
In May 2019, as sanctions grew tighter and relief efforts such as INSTEX had yet to bring relief, Rouhani announced that Iran would begin pulling back from its JCPOA commitments. As time went on, the country gradually increased the number of commitments it would abrogate, but Rouhani said these measures would be reversed if the other signatories to the deal began offering relief to Iran’s energy and finance sectors, as promised in the JCPOA agreement.
In reaction to the sanctions, Iran was involved in a number of standoffs and attacks in the region. Many of these incidents involved ships in the Gulf of Oman, but other incidents occurred as well. After a U.S. spy drone was shot down in June, the United States nearly retaliated with air strikes before the operation was called off at the last minute. In September two Saudi Aramco oil-processing facilities suffered an attack, apparently originating from Iran but claimed by its Houthi rebel allies in Yemen.
In mid-November, with sanctions biting, the Iranian government raised the country’s heavily subsidized fuel prices. Cities across the country erupted in protests almost immediately, and security forces responded with a brutal crackdown that was accompanied by an unprecedented 
Meanwhile, unrelated protests in neighboring Iraq began to take aim at Iran for meddling in Iraqi affairs, and on November 27 the Iranian consulate in the Iraqi city of Najaf was burned down. A month later, after an Iraqi militia with Iranian backing attacked an Iraqi air base hosting U.S. personnel, the United States conducted air strikes against that militia. On January 3, 2020, the commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, Qassem Soleimani, arrived at Baghdad International Airport to meet a commander of that Iraqi militia. Both were killed at the airport by an air strike from the United States.
Iran terminated most of its remaining commitments to the JCPOA in the days following the air strike, pointing to the inability of the other signatories to uphold their end of the deal and invoking a provision within the agreement that was meant to serve as a dispute mechanism. On January 8, as a direct retaliation for the killing of Soleimani, Iran launched several ballistic missiles toward Iraqi bases hosting U.S. troops, which caused dozens of injuries but no deaths.
That same night, the Revolutionary Guards mistook Ukraine International Airlines flight 752, a passenger flight headed to Kyiv from Tehran, for a cruise missile. The corps shot down the airplane, killing all 176 people on board. The incident kindled recollections of downed Iran Air flight 655 in 1988, sparking anti-government protests across Iran. Iran, eventually accepting responsibility, agreed to compensate the families of the victims but failed to hold any public officials accountable.
Throughout 2020 Iran saw a number of other setbacks that appeared to target its missile development and military capabilities. In June and July several facilities, some of them part of the country’s missile program, suffered fires and explosions. In November a top nuclear expert and a Revolutionary Guards commander were killed in separate attacks. Responsibility for the explosions and assassinations remained unclear.
As tensions escalated, so too Iran accelerated its nuclear development. By November 2020 its stockpile of enriched uranium had reached 12 times the level that had been permitted under the JCPOA. In January 2021 it began enriching uranium up to 20 percent purity; under the JCPOA it had been capped at 3.67 percent.
Negotiations to return the United States to the agreement began in early April 2021, some two months after the inauguration U.S. Pres. Joe Biden, and continued until June, when Ebrahim Raisi was elected president. They resumed in late November, by which time Iran had enriched uranium up to 60 percent purity and had reduced its breakout window for producing a nuclear weapon to two to three months.
Raisi’s presidency, meanwhile, was marked by a flurry of diplomatic outreach. Apart from fostering relations with regional neighbors, especially including countries of Central Asia, Raisi strengthened cooperation with China, which continued to import large amounts of Iranian oil despite U.S. sanctions. He also initiated reconciliation talks with Saudi Arabia in 2022, after diplomatic relations between the Middle East rivals had been severed amid tensions in 2016. Later that year he hosted a high-profile summit with Turkey and Russia to address the outstanding issues of the Syrian Civil War, highlighting Iran’s continued relevance in shaping the region’s future. Meanwhile, Iran supplied Russia with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs; also called drones), ballistic missiles, and other war matériel used to fight the war in Ukraine.
Mounting conflict and a regime embattled
Tensions with Israel grew more pronounced after October 7, 2023, when Hamas, a Palestinian militant movement in the Gaza Strip, launched the deadliest attack on Israel since its independence in 1948 and took civilian hostages for the first time. Israel responded with devastating force while the Iran-led Axis of Resistance—which included Hamas in the Gaza Strip, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Houthi forces in Yemen—stepped up attacks on Israel. In April 2024 Iran and Israel came into direct confrontation after an Israeli strike on Iran’s embassy complex in Damascus killed, among others, senior officers of the IRGC. Two weeks later Iran fired hundreds of drones and missiles into Israeli air space; Israel responded in kind by attacking a military complex near Isfahan. Iran downplayed the incident, bringing the escalation to a virtual close, though Raisi continued to take a hard line in his public rhetoric.
In the wake of the confrontation, Raisi embarked on a previously scheduled tour to Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Azerbaijan, where he discussed and inaugurated joint infrastructure projects. On the way to Tabriz from Azerbaijan, his helicopter crashed into the mountainous terrain in Iran’s East Azerbaijan province, killing Raisi, Iran’s foreign minister, and the seven other people aboard the flight.
The election of Masoud Pezeshkian to replace Raisi was taken by some observers as a softening of Iran’s stance toward the West. But Pezeshkian had hardly taken office before the regime had to brace to maintain a hard line. Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh was assassinated by a covert Israeli operation in Tehran just hours after he attended Pezeshkian’s inauguration. Less than two months later, Israeli forces killed Hassan Nasrallah, the leader of Hezbollah and one of Iran’s most important allies in the region. Iran responded by launching 180 ballistic missiles toward Israel in another brief round of confrontation between the two countries.
The Axis of Resistance was dealt a serious blow, as did Iran’s posture in the region. Hezbollah was severely weakened by Nasrallah’s death and weeks of subsequent conflict in Lebanon. The militant group’s retreat from the Syrian Civil War allowed Syrian rebels to swiftly topple Pres. Bashar al-Assad, another key ally of Iran, and put in place a transitional government in December that was firmly opposed to Iranian interference in Syria.
After Trump returned to the U.S. presidency in January 2025, the United States renewed threats to hold Iran accountable for the activities of its allies and pressured Iran into renewed negotiations over its nuclear program, ballistic missiles, and regional activity. Negotiations began in April and staved off an Israeli operation on Iran that was planned for that month. But the negotiations fell apart abruptly in June and, days later, Israel launched an attack on Iran that disabled its air defense systems, killed top military leaders and nuclear scientists, and caused significant damage to its nuclear facilities. In the final days of the 12-Day War, U.S. B-2 bombers dropped U.S. GBU-57 A/B “bunker buster” bombs on nuclear facilities in Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan, an attack which Trump said was intended to be a limited, one-off mission.

articles.title: Riyadh's dilemma: Can Saudi Arabia stop Houthi attacks without triggering a wider war? - analysis - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Riyadh's dilemma: Can Saudi Arabia stop Houthi attacks without triggering a wider war? - analysis  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
The deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the last week have put pressure on Riyadh to respond.
Saudi Arabia has carried out airstrikes on the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government forces over the past month. However, Riyadh has appeared reticent to respond in a massive way to the Houthi attacks. Rumors are swirling in the region about what might come next. Analysts tend to portray the Saudis as facing an uphill struggle with the Houthis.
Does Saudi Arabia really have no good options? Various recent reports have discussed different aspects of what Riyadh may be weighing in terms of what comes next.
For instance, there is the question of the US supporting Saudi Arabia. The US and many countries have condemned the attacks. However, US President Donald Trump has left media guessing as to whether the US will do more. The US appears to be supporting Saudi Arabia in terms of intelligence and targeting, according to the BBC.
The Houthis have threatened a "swift and painful" response if the US does intervene. "If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told the AFP.
All of this must weigh on US-Saudi coordination. There are questions about how a widening war in Yemen could also lead Iran to operationalize militias in Iraq.
Who should Saudi Arabia ally with to minimize spread of war in the Middle East?
Saudi Arabia has seen this before. It intervened in Yemen in 2015 to back the Yemeni government against the Houthis. The Houthis widened the war with ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. In 2019, Iran directly attacked Saudi Arabia. Militias in Iraq also targeted Saudi Arabia. Therefore, Riyadh knows exactly what is at stake.
Meanwhile, there are questions about whether tensions in Yemen could lead to renewed fighting with Iran. Reports indicate that Israel could be involved in strikes on Iran again, or even on the Houthis.
There is intense interest in this among Saudi Arabia’s allies in Turkey and Pakistan. Those countries joined an alliance with Saudi Arabia over the last few months.
However, Turkey would likely not want to be on the same side as Israel fighting alongside Saudi Arabia. Anadolu media in Ankara noted that Riyadh had so far rejected Israel’s “bid to join fight.” It is not entirely clear if Israel wants to get deeply involved again in Yemen.
Israel already carried out strikes on Yemen in 2024-2025 in response to numerous attacks by the Houthis on Israel. The Houthis also attacked commercial ships they claimed were linked to Israel. They seized the Galaxy Leader, only releasing the crew in 2025. They tried to make the ship into a kind of tourist attraction. The Galaxy Leader finally partially sank in April 2026, the Maritime Executive noted.
How did Saudi Arabia get into tensions with the Houthis?
Further context might help explain how Riyadh got here.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in March 2015, leading a coalition against the Iranian-backed Houthis after the group seized Sanaa and advanced toward Aden. The intervention developed into a prolonged conflict involving airstrikes, ground fighting and Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory. A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 significantly reduced hostilities, and although it formally expired that October, a fragile period of relative calm followed.
That ceasefire has come under increasing pressure in 2026. Saudi strikes on Sanaa in July marked a renewed escalation, while the Houthis subsequently launched an offensive toward Bab el-Mandeb, the strategic strait connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. It’s worth recalling that Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government did not want Sanaa airport used by Iran to fly in Iranian advisers to the Houthis.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched a counteroffensive in October, supported by coalition airstrikes, to recover territory near Bab el-Mandeb and Mocha. The Houthis also escalated attacks on Saudi airports, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where an October 10 strike killed 12 people and wounded 309. Riyadh vowed a firm response.
The conflict has also expanded beyond Yemen. On September 11, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones that Saudi and Iraqi authorities said originated in Iraq. Riyadh temporarily shut the pipeline, a crucial alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The attack highlighted growing concerns about coordination among Iran-backed terrorist groups across the region and the potential vulnerability of Saudi energy infrastructure.
On October 12, JINSA President and CEO Michael Makovsky spoke to Fox News about the latest Houthi attacks. “It’s very important that the [Saudi] Crown Prince be successful [in combating the Houthis], and it’s vital for US national security. But he’s alienated or distanced himself from a few key countries that could have been helpful here. I mean, he had a very well-known fight with the Emiratis, who were effective ... against the Houthis. ... He’s kept a distance from the Israelis, who have ... [been] very effective at hitting the Houthis, and, at times in this war, he’s been rather cool to the United States,” Makovsky said, according to a synopsis of the discussion released by JINSA.
He added, “I’d like to see the Saudis work with the Israelis, the Emiratis, and the US to deal with the Houthi threat. It is not only a threat to the Saudis, of course, but affects the whole world because of [the Houthi threat] to international commerce. ... There has to be an international coalition.”
Thomas Juneau, a Professor at the University of Ottawa, who focuses on Iran and Yemen and is a former Department of National Defense analyst in Canada, noted on October 11 on X that “Saudi Arabia faces no good options with the Houthis. Military escalation was inevitable and is likely to continue–but it will hurt Saudi Arabia more than the Houthis. Negotiations are inevitable too–though not in the short term. The Houthis hold stronger cards, and they know it; their goal will be to extract maximal concessions from Saudi Arabia, which remains reluctant to pay this very high price.”
Game theory can help Saudi Arabia face its Houthi dilemma
Might game theory help us understand the dilemma for Saudi Arabia in confronting the Houthis? The challenge is assessing how this spectacle connects with Iran, Israel, the United States, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan.
The central problem is that Saudi Arabia may be militarily stronger than the Houthis, but military superiority does not necessarily translate into strategic leverage. The Houthis can impose high costs on Saudi Arabia without defeating its armed forces. Riyadh, meanwhile, must consider how its response affects not only Yemen but its economic security, regional alliances, and relations with Iran. This is what is called an “asymmetric” conflict.
This creates several overlapping strategic dilemmas. Saudi Arabia faces three calculations it has to make at the same time. It has to examine how it might deter more attacks, it has to manage its alliances, and it has to look at the regional context and potential escalation. Game theory does not provide a clear answer, because the outcomes depend on uncertain information, different objectives, and the decisions of several independent actors. Nevertheless, it might be helpful to model this problem more because Saudi Arabia is in a difficult position, but it has many options.
Saudi Arabia can weather the storm. It has done so in the past. It has a naturally cautious leadership, like most Gulf countries. The West tends to prefer quick solutions, and Western media appears to think that the lack of an immediate large response, like “shock and awe,” means nothing is happening. However, this illustrates the differences in calculations. The Iran war, for instance, has proven to be longer and more complex than many thought. This reflects differences in thinking between Washington, Jerusalem, Riyadh, Ankara, and other places in the region.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking Saudi Arabia's approval to launch airstrikes against Yemen's pro-Iran Houthi rebels, the Israeli daily Haaretz reported on the 13th (local time), citing diplomatic sources.
According to the report, Prime Minister Netanyahu is seeking Saudi permission, mediated by the United States, so that Israel can intervene in the decade-long civil war in Yemen.
This is interpreted as an intention by Israel to advance relations with Saudi Arabia and ultimately lay the groundwork for a diplomatic normalization agreement.
The strategy appears to exploit Saudi Arabia's difficult position amid the Houthis' offensive, which has gained control over the Red Sea region with unprecedented military capability and even threatened the Saudi mainland.
However, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Kingdom's de facto ruler, is reportedly reluctant to grant permission, concerned that Israel's military intervention would negatively impact domestic public opinion.
Given that Crown Prince Mohammed currently serves as Saudi Prime Minister, the likelihood of Israel's intervention materializing without his final approval remains slim.
Prime Minister Netanyahu, who signed the Abraham Accords with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco in 2020 during the first term of U.S. President Donald Trump, has long sought to expand the accords by normalizing relations with Saudi Arabia, the leader of the Sunni Islamic world.
However, Saudi Arabia has delayed normalization with Israel, citing the resolution of the Palestinian issue and other reasons.
Saudi Arabia maintains its stance that it can only normalize relations with Israel once an independent Palestinian state is established.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Netanyahu has repeatedly stated through recent election campaigns and other occasions that he cannot accept the establishment of a Palestinian state.

Reaffirms support for kingdom’s security and sovereignty; urges full compliance with the Gaza ceasefire
Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes while reaffirming its unwavering support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan’s Acting Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, expressed deep concern over the rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen.
He said Pakistan backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to revive dialogue aimed at securing a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Statement by Ambassador Usman Jadoon,
Acting Permanent Representative of Pakistan to the UN,
At the UN Security Council Open Debate on the Situation in the Middle East
(15 October 2026)

Madam President,
I thank Acting Special Coordinator – Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov for… pic.twitter.com/UJyj2sVlYY
— Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the UN (@PakistanUN_NY) October 15, 2026
The ambassador strongly condemned continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including its civilian and economic infrastructure, and called for an immediate halt to the strikes.
“We reiterate our unwavering support for the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the brotherly Kingdom, and reaffirm its right to self-defence under international law against any external attacks,” he said.
The condemnation comes amid an escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others. Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia was also targeted amid renewed hostilities.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have since claimed hundreds of strikes on Houthi-held territory. The Houthis say the attacks have killed civilians, including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
The Saudis entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine.
A 2022 ceasefire reached by the Saudis and the Houthis unravelled this summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.
Jadoon said that Pakistan remains committed to advancing dialogue and diplomacy in the region to help de-escalate tensions, resolve differences and promote lasting peace and stability in the region.
Turning to the Palestinian issue, the ambassador said the two-state solution remained the internationally agreed framework and an indispensable foundation for a just and lasting peace.
“This international commitment to the two-State solution must be accompanied by concrete measures to preserve the territorial integrity and viability of the State of Palestine,” he said, while expressing support for the full and good-faith implementation of relevant UN resolutions and the New York Declaration.
Expressing concern over Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, he said settlement expansion, particularly the E1 project, threatened to sever Palestinian territorial contiguity.
“Settler violence, demolitions, land seizures and forced displacement are entrenching annexation and dismantling the foundations of peace,” he said.
He called for an end to all settlement activities in accordance with relevant UN resolutions, a halt to settler violence and accountability for those responsible.
E1, which stands for “East 1”, is an area east of Jerusalem between East Jerusalem and the large Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. Experts have warned that the project could divide land the Palestinians hope will form part of an independent state, threatening the possibility of a two-state solution.
Jadoon also strongly condemned what he described as provocative and illegal incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque/Al-Haram Al-Sharif and called for respect for the historical and legal status quo of the holy sites.
He said continued ceasefire violations, the killing of Palestinians and restrictions on humanitarian access in Gaza remained a matter of grave concern.
The approaching winter threatened to worsen the suffering of families living amid widespread destruction without adequate shelter or essential services, he added.

“The ceasefire must be fully upheld, humanitarian assistance delivered unhindered and at scale, and recovery and reconstruction advanced without delay,” he said, stressing that the indispensable work of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) must be supported.
Pakistan rejected forced displacement and any attempt to fragment Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which, he said, constituted a single territorial unit.
The ambassador also called for the release of withheld Palestinian revenues to enable the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its responsibilities.
He said collective efforts must focus on a credible, time-bound and irreversible political process to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable State of Palestine on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.
“This remains the only credible foundation for a just and lasting resolution of the Palestinian question,” he said.
“So long as the occupation continues and the Palestinian people’s legitimate yearning for self-determination goes unfulfilled, lasting peace in the Middle East will remain out of reach,” he said, reaffirming Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Palestinian people.
On Lebanon, Jadoon said full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution, respect for the cessation of hostilities and Israel’s withdrawal from occupied territory remained essential.
He said the Lebanese government’s call for the continuation of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and a sustained UN presence in the country merited serious and favourable consideration by the Security Council.
On Syria, Pakistan welcomed the government’s efforts to foster internal stability and put the country on a positive trajectory.
“We reaffirm support for Syria’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity,” he said, adding that the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and Security Council resolutions 338 and 497 must be fully respected.

articles.title: Analysis-How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively? - WTVB
articles.summary: Analysis-How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?  WTVB
articles.full_text:
By John Davison
LONDON, Oct 15 (Reuters) – Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.
The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.
This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say.
They attribute Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to a ragtag group of Yemeni fighters to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, and the impact of the US war on Iran that has depleted stocks of interceptors.
TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN
Iran has been giving weapons, money and training to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo.
While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran’s other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King’s College London.
“Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities,” he said.
“Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted.”
Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran.
“The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn’t receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces,” said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles.
“Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish,” Nikou said.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told a press conference the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of “regional actors,” including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.
DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY
A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don’t rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran.
The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen’s internationally recognised government seized one such shipment.
“China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially,” Krieg said.
The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons’ effectiveness.
Anthropic said last month that “a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen” had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle.
WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS
While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular.
“Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do,” said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute.
Saudi Arabia’s sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said.
WAR EXPERIENCE
The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said.
A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea.
The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities.
“They haven’t been sitting still,” Sabet said. “They were basically diversifying their supply chains… and as they gain operational experience, they’re able to make those weapons more sophisticated.”
(Reporting and writing by John Davison; Editing by Alex Richardson)

articles.title: Houthi attacks disrupt Pakistani IT firms’ business in Saudi Arabia, executives say - Arab News PK
articles.summary: Houthi attacks disrupt Pakistani IT firms’ business in Saudi Arabia, executives say  Arab News PK
articles.full_text:
- Prolonged instability threatens growth in Pakistan’s $4.6 billion technology export sector
- Executives report delayed projects and stalled investments as security concerns mount
ISLAMABAD: Pakistani technology firms operating in Saudi Arabia said this week Houthi attacks on the Kingdom are disrupting business, delaying projects and holding up new investments, threatening growth in one of Pakistan’s most important overseas IT markets.
The warnings follow a series of deadly attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, including a strike on Saturday that killed 12 people and injured 309, followed by another on Sunday that killed a Pakistani national and wounded 11 others.
The disruption comes as Saudi Arabia emerges as an increasingly important market for Pakistani technology companies, driven by the Kingdom’s investments in digital infrastructure, cloud computing and enterprise services under its Vision 2030 economic diversification program. Pakistan’s technology exports reached a record $4.6 billion in the fiscal year ended June 2026, up 21 percent from a year earlier.
Executives interviewed by Arab News said Saudi clients were reviewing budgets, postponing investments and delaying decisions on new projects as uncertainty over the security situation grows, potentially affecting Pakistani companies’ earnings and future expansion.
“Regarding the current situation, it is quite unpredictable at the moment,” said Shumail Haider, country head of the IT division at Jeddah-based Typical Solution. “Companies are being affected in one way or another. The whole ecosystem … is being affected.”
“Specifically, for the IT companies … there was a lot of investment expected, which is on hold now,” he added. “The existing projects have been paused and new projects are being delayed.”
Haider said the attacks were compounding pressures from regional tensions, supply chain disruptions and higher fuel costs, making it harder for businesses to plan investments and maintain normal operations.
Saad Shah, founder and chief executive of Hexalyze, an enterprise technology consultancy with an office in Riyadh, said Saudi Arabia’s reputation for safety had been a major attraction for Pakistani firms seeking to establish themselves in the Kingdom.
But the recent attacks had introduced uncertainty, prompting some corporate clients to reassess their spending plans, he said.
“We work with large enterprises,” Shah said, explaining that such companies generally operate within predetermined budgets.
“Most of the organizations are thinking of cutting their budget according to their situation,” he added, saying the spending reviews were directly affecting his business.
Shah cautioned that it was too early to assess the full commercial impact of the attacks, although he said business activity had already slowed as companies evaluated the security situation.
The potential consequences are significant for Pakistan, which has increasingly relied on technology services to expand exports and earn foreign exchange.
Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said in July Pakistan’s information and communications technology exports had risen 21 percent to $4.6 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year, reflecting growing overseas demand for Pakistani software, outsourcing and digital services.
Saudi Arabia has become an important destination for Pakistani technology companies and freelancers seeking contracts in a market undergoing rapid digital transformation.
“Saudi Arabia is a major market for the Pakistan IT industry as well as for the freelancers,” Shah said. “If the region is affected due to war and this sort of situation, definitely the export growth will be slow for the next year.”
The risks extend beyond technology exports because Saudi Arabia is also Pakistan’s largest source of workers’ remittances, making any prolonged disruption to employment and business activity a concern for the wider economy.
Pakistan received nearly $10.9 billion in remittances during the first quarter of the current fiscal year, including $899.1 million from Saudi Arabia in September alone, according to central bank figures.
Shah said large numbers of Pakistanis worked in Saudi Arabia across construction, finance, health care and technology, while more Pakistani businesses had established local offices to serve Saudi clients.
A prolonged slowdown could affect companies’ export earnings and, if it spread to employment, the incomes of Pakistani expatriates. Neither executive, however, provided estimates of potential financial losses or reported job cuts linked to the attacks.
Haider said the longer the instability persisted, the greater the potential damage to investment and commercial activity.
“We hope this would settle down soon, but it seems that if it does not, then we will have far more effect than it is right now,” he said.

articles.summary: Israeli forces have arrested more than 2,000 Palestinian children since the onset of its genocidal Gaza war, with at least 350 remaining in custody under severe conditions, the Pal...
articles.full_text:
Israeli forces have arrested more than 2,000 Palestinian children since the onset of its genocidal Gaza war, with at least 350 remaining in custody under severe conditions, the Palestinian Prisoners Society said Wednesday.
The non-governmental organization that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.
Monitoring and documentation indicate that "more than 2,000 children have been arrested since the start of the genocide on October 2023, while at least 350 remain in detention under harsh conditions," it said.
The group warned of an escalation in the targeting of Palestinian children through practices including intimidation, arrest, torture, starvation, isolation and denial of health care.
It added that information on the number of children detained from the Gaza Strip since the start of the war remains unclear, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of "enforced disappearance."
The group said Israel’s administrative detention policy, under which Palestinian detainees are held without a publicly stated charge or a clear timeframe for release, leaves children facing an uncertain future and deprives them of family and educational stability.
It also said Israeli courts contribute to the continuation of violations against children amid the absence of effective accountability.
The Palestinian Prisoners Society cited the case of child Walid Khaled Ahmad, who "died in Megiddo Prison in March 2025, amid medical findings at the time indicating severe emaciation and signs of malnutrition and dehydration."
The group raised questions about accountability for his death, noting that the investigation into the case had been closed.
It also highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who it said developed scabies while detained in Ofer Prison, leading to a deterioration in his health and serious infections affecting vital organs.
Hamid underwent heart surgeries and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition before one of his legs was later amputated, the group said.
It added that Hamid has continued receiving treatment for about three months since Israeli authorities released him following the deterioration of his health, a move the group described as "an evasion of responsibility for his medical care."
The group called for international action to secure the release of children held arbitrarily, end administrative detention and coercive interrogations, and stop torture, starvation and the denial of medical treatment.
It stressed the need to move beyond documentation and condemnation toward concrete measures that end the violations and bring impunity to an end, saying that "protecting Palestinian children requires firm international intervention to ensure respect for their rights, lives and dignity."
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in the Israeli genocide since October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli army raids and attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s genocide against the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

articles.title: Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film  Al JazeeraNAZA film review — Israeli accounts of assault on Gaza make brutally hard viewing  Financial TimesA Gaza war documentary sparks outrage in Israel  NPRNAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees  The GuardianInside NAZA, the documentary no Israeli cinema will show  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.full_text:
An Al Jazeera investigation has exposed holes in claims that an Israeli counter-film to the acclaimed documentary NAZA achieved more than 44 million views. By examining domain registries, web archives, source code, and three independent traffic tools, the investigation exposed the fabricated numbers adopted by official Israeli entities to promote the film.
The original award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers, accusing the army of using artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems to kill numerous civilians in Gaza. The documentary takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes. After winning the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the film was scheduled to screen in 56 countries.
Recommended Stories
Official backlash
The success of the original documentary triggered a political storm in Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants and prosecute them for information security violations.
The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, were accused of treason, and Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.
Network of domains
To counter the film’s global resonance, opponents created a counter-film. On September 16, just days after NAZA premiered, the domain nazadocumentary.com was registered via Cloudflare, with the owner’s details hidden.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine revealed the site initially disguised itself as the official NAZA website, listing the directors’ names and information on screenings and press. However, it described the film as exposing the systems behind the calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza. By September 30, this deceptive page vanished, replaced by a new title, “NAZA: The Real Story”.
The individuals behind the 49-minute counter-film are Ariel Averbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman, who claimed the work was self-funded. Later, two more domains, whatisnaza.com and watchnaza.com, were registered to redirect users to the counter-film.
The fake counter
By the morning of October 14, the nazadocumentary.com website’s counter displayed 43,758,421 views, without disclosing the source of the number or how it was calculated.
Public platforms told a drastically different story. The full 49-minute version of the film on its official YouTube channel had not exceeded 130,000 views by the same date. This means the website’s counter displayed roughly 336 times the actual viewership. The YouTube channel had fewer than 2,000 subscribers, and the film’s account on X had only 170 followers.
Independent traffic analysis platforms confirmed the discrepancy. The US-based platform Semrush estimated the site’s total visits by October 8 at about half a million. Israeli-founded Similarweb estimated only 326 visits for September. Furthermore, the film’s domains were absent from the Tranco list of the world’s top one million visited domains.
Discrepancies and code
An examination of the page’s source code revealed that the element displaying the huge number was internally tagged as “visitors” but displayed to users as “views”. The number is delivered directly from the site’s server, making its calculation method invisible from the outside. Upon opening the page, the counter begins at 97 percent of its value and counts up for three seconds, creating the illusion of a live counter.
Additionally, the site collects actual viewing data without publishing it, sending a “watch-tracker” file after about 25 seconds of video playback to identify the viewing session and parts watched, leaving it unknown whether the counter is based on this data.
State promotion
Despite the seemingly fabricated metrics, official Israeli accounts spearheaded the promotion of the counter-film. The Israeli Embassy in Washington promoted it on October 3 on social media.
Tzipi Hotovely, head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, awarded the three creators certificates of recognition for countering the original film. Hotovely said the film had garnered tens of millions of views, transforming an unsupported, fabricated number into an official talking point.
This elaborate digital campaign unfolds against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Since the conflict started, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

articles.title: Iran mulls tactical shift in Hormuz attacks before key US vote
articles.summary: Iran is using new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz to maintain high oil prices and influence the U.S. midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. T...
articles.full_text:
Iran is using new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz to maintain high oil prices and influence the U.S. midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the U.S. vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
A U.S. military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the U.S. destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including U.S. naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the U.S. military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. U.S. forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the U.S. official said.
Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after U.S. strikes devastated its navy.
The war – and its $3 billion monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the U.S. campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.
The U.S. has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.
In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.
There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on Oct. 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the U.N. shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.
"There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said.
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
"Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said.
"Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz."
The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said.
In its latest report on Sunday, the U.S. Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe," the second-highest level.
"IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

articles.title: Saudi coalition fighting Houthis intercepts missile near Medina
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Thursday it intercepted a cruise missile over the Medina region, home to Islam's second-holiest city, which the rebels had pre...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Thursday it intercepted a cruise missile over the Medina region, home to Islam's second-holiest city, which the rebels had previously pledged to spare.
"Interception and destruction of a cruise missile in the Medina region," coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki wrote on X, with the statement also published by state media.
The statement did not identify who launched the missile or its intended target and provided no details on possible casualties or damage.
However, it came amid intensified Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting airports and energy facilities.
Responding to the announcement, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied that the group had carried out any attacks against Saudi Arabia on Thursday.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces confirm that they have not carried out any operation targeting Saudi territory today," Saree said, referring to the group's forces.
Earlier Sept. 29, the coalition also accused the Houthis of carrying out a drone attack on the Taibah electricity distribution station in Medina.
The attack knocked a transformer out of service but did not disrupt the electricity grid, according to al-Maliki. The facility supplies electricity to the Prophet's Mosque.
Thursday's incident came hours after the coalition said early Thursday that it intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province.
A day earlier, the coalition announced that it had destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the rebels toward the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Houthis since 2015. The group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.

articles.title: 5 killed in Yemen palace strike as Houthis claim hit on Saudi jet
articles.summary: At least five people were killed and 16 wounded Thursday when Yemen's Houthi forces struck the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden, as the group also claimed t...
articles.full_text:
At least five people were killed and 16 wounded Thursday when Yemen's Houthi forces struck the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden, as the group also claimed to have hit a Saudi fighter jet amid escalating hostilities with the Saudi-led coalition.
The missile and drone attack targeted Al-Maashiq palace, the headquarters of Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government, marking the first such strike on the complex in the latest round of fighting.
Yemeni Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included security guards and civilian employees, while Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani confirmed that the prime minister and Cabinet members were unharmed.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for the attack, saying the group had targeted what it described as a Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden.
The Houthi-run SABA news agency alleged that Saudi officers operated the facility and that it housed weapons depots, claims that could not be independently verified.
Meanwhile, the Houthis released footage purportedly showing a missile striking a Royal Saudi Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon over Yemen's northern Saada province late Wednesday.
Saree claimed the fighter jet, which reportedly departed from Saudi Arabia's Taif Air Base, had been directly hit and was at risk of crashing.
However, the infrared footage appeared to show a missile detonating near the aircraft rather than striking it directly, with the pilot apparently maneuvering away from the explosion.
A visible trail from the aircraft's left wing raised speculation about possible damage from missile fragments, although neither the extent of any damage nor the authenticity of the footage could be independently confirmed.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the incident, and there have been no verified reports of a fighter jet being shot down.
The missile involved was believed by some observers to be a Barq surface-to-air missile, a weapon associated with Houthi air defense systems and reportedly linked to Iranian missile technology.
The alleged engagement came as Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of intensifying missile and drone attacks against airports, ports and energy infrastructure across the kingdom.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said Thursday that Houthi forces had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others.
Separate attacks on Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia killed three people and wounded 28, according to the coalition.
Maliki accused the Houthis of acquiring advanced weapons, including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden boats, with assistance from regional actors.
He also said coalition forces had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen.
The coalition separately announced that it had intercepted and destroyed drones over Khamis Mushait and another area in southern Saudi Arabia.
Following the developments, the Houthis warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, excluding the airspace above the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed violence follows the collapse of a prolonged lull in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year.
Fighting resumed last month amid a broader regional conflict that erupted following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Yemeni government forces have since launched operations to recapture Houthi-held territory, including areas near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for international shipping.
Humanitarian organizations have warned that the renewed fighting risks worsening Yemen's already severe humanitarian crisis.

articles.title: Israel–US Strategic Cooperation Against Iran: Limits And Divergences – Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Israel–US Strategic Cooperation Against Iran: Limits And Divergences – Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
By Dr. Hirak Jyoti Das
Key Takeaways:
- The joint US-Israeli war against Iran failed to deliver regime change or the destruction of Tehran’s nuclear and missile capabilities, exposing divergences over means, timing and acceptable costs, especially after the June 2026 memorandum of understanding restrained Israel’s direct role.
- Washington, facing mid-term electoral pressure, high costs and oil-price spikes above $100 a barrel, has shifted toward coercive diplomacy focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and limited nuclear restrictions, while Israel continues to prioritise sustained degradation of Iran and Hezbollah and opposes any deal that restores Tehran’s bargaining power.
- The article concludes that the conflict is likely to settle into prolonged, managed low-intensity confrontation or partial negotiated de-escalation, with Israel retaining the option of unilateral actions in Lebanon or sabotage inside Iran if US concessions are judged insufficient.
Israel and the US launched a war against Iran based on strategic convergences around regime change, degradation of Iran’s nuclear, military and missile capabilities, and non-state networks. The failure to achieve these objectives alongside Iran’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, retaliatory strikes on Gulf states and the ability to influence Lebanon’s future, exposed differences between Israel and the US over the means, timing and acceptable costs of pursuing the said goals.
Following the 17 June 2026 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Washington and Tehran, the US restrained Israel’s direct involvement in Iran, limiting its role to intelligence cooperation and allowing calibrated military efforts in Lebanon to weaken Hezbollah. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu noted that joint military efforts succeeded in deterring Iran’s immediate nuclear threat, severely damaging Iran’s missiles, military and non-state networks and vowed to hold security zones in Lebanon, Gaza and Syria indefinitely to ensure the Jewish state’s security.[1]
The US has pressed for diplomacy over the nuclear issue while continuing its war of attrition against Iran, with the battleground shifting to the Strait of Hormuz amid disputes over control of the vital waterway, triggering renewed strikes targeting military and critical infrastructure.[2] Israel welcomed the MoU’s collapse, advocating continued full-scale joint war efforts to translate military gains into strategic outcomes. Therefore, the war has reflected divergences in interpretation of the Iranian challenge between Israel and the US over Lebanon, the Strait of Hormuz, and the nuclear and missile programme.[3]
US’ Changing Priorities
President Donald Trump, after launching the war, anticipated a swift and decisive victory, seeking access to its oil and other resources, influence over Iran’s leadership transition, and cultivation of pro-Western ‘moderates’ favouring change from within the Islamic regime to avoid a power vacuum, instability or civil war.[4] In the absence of decisive victory, Washington pursued containment, deterrence, coercive diplomacy and strategic bargaining, combining military, economic and political pressure, including infrastructure disruption, sanctions and phased concessions, diplomatic timelines and inspections, to compel renewed negotiations over ceasefires, maritime access and the nuclear programme.[5]
Washington situates Iran within a broader strategic environment, assessing the potential costs across other theatres and dynamics involving China, Russia and its Gulf allies.[6] Therefore, Washington seeks to avoid prolonged, large-scale military engagement, particularly ground operations amid the upcoming mid-term elections, Congressional scrutiny, budgetary pressures costing US$ 45.1 billion between 28 February and mid-September 2026 and public opposition, including from Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) base, to new wars.[7] Rising perceptions that Trump was manipulated into a costly “war of choice” have reframed the Netanyahu government as a liability, intensifying demands to re-assess military aid to Israel.[8]
Trump’s military objectives evolved from regime change and unconditional surrender to securing the Strait of Hormuz and nuclear non-proliferation, creating ambiguity that enabled him to declare victory despite a lack of transformational change.[9] Nevertheless, the failure compelled Washington to prioritise containing the conflict’s spillover, particularly by reopening the Strait of Hormuz, preserving global oil market stability and deterring retaliation against the energy facilities of the Gulf States.[10] Disruptions to international shipping, which have heightened inflationary pressures, have pushed Brent crude prices above US$ 100 per barrel. The tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s retaliatory attacks on US allies have undermined Washington’s power projection, testing the reliability of its security guarantees and ability to safeguard maritime access.
The war has reduced Iran’s incentives to offer nuclear concessions as the naval blockade strengthens its bargaining position, and preserving nuclear capabilities provides a potential deterrent in the future. The US seeks destruction, removal or down-blending of a 440 kg highly-enriched Uranium stockpile outside Iran, a 20-year suspension of enrichment activities and stringent restrictions on nuclear facilities and sanctions relief tied to verifiable compliance. These objectives remain unfulfilled through both military and diplomatic means.
With limited leverage following the failure to guarantee maritime access and prevent attacks on Gulf States, Washington may increasingly favour a limited agreement involving Iran’s commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, negotiations on exporting or down-blending highly-enriched Uranium, a time-bound enrichment suspension and phased implementation of sanctions relief.[11] However, without reaching common ground, the ongoing low-intensity conflict could continue. Moreover, Trump considers Iran’s ballistic missiles a critical challenge but not an existential threat to Israel, and seeks to prevent the issue from complicating nuclear negotiations.[12]
Israel’s Objectives
Israel conceptualises Iran as an immediate, geographically proximate and multi-dimensional challenge, encompassing ideological hostility, missile and cyber capabilities and an allied network, calling any delay in tackling this threat inherently risky. Israel views even a ‘near-nuclear’ Iran as capable of altering the tactics of allied groups, constraining the operational freedom of the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) and eroding deterrence. Israel’s approach stems from a low threat-tolerance threshold arising from limited strategic depth and acute vulnerability to missiles, drones and infiltration attempts, favouring proactively neutralising immediate and long-term threats.[13] Israel endeavours to exploit Iran’s diminished military status and fractured support networks through sustained mowing-the-grass operations, degrading defensive capabilities, dismantling its nuclear and ballistic missile sites and severing ties with allied groups.[14]
Israel’s strategic objective is to remove the Islamic regime, leave Iran weakened and fragmented, preclude future threats to the Jewish state and reshape the balance of power. While the US has avoided uncontrolled escalation that could create a power vacuum and refrained from attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure, thereby limiting disruptions to global energy markets, Israel has pursued a more direct regime decapitation strategy, including high-profile assassinations and strikes on critical economic infrastructure such as oil refineries, storage facilities and pipelines.
By killing senior leaders, Israel aims to disrupt Iran’s command-and-control and political decision-making, generate internal instability and create conditions for regime collapse, despite the risks of regional and international instability. For Israel, returning to negotiations before resolving fundamental issues risks allowing Iran to rebuild its capabilities and reassert regional influence. The Netanyahu government has therefore sought to sabotage negotiations and derail any agreement.[15]
For Israel, the economic costs of the Strait of Hormuz’s closure are less consequential than for the US. While Trump is increasingly focused on the conflict’s economic implications, Netanyahu remains focused on security. Consequently, re-opening the Strait of Hormuz is a low priority for Israel, which is more concerned with Iran leveraging the waterway for strategic concessions and bargaining advantage.[16]
On the nuclear issue, Israel objected to deferring negotiations under the June 2026 MoU, given the US’ priority of re-opening the Strait of Hormuz. According to the Israeli perspective, the war should have facilitated a re-negotiated nuclear agreement on terms heavily favouring the Israel–US axis. While broadly aligned with US’ non-proliferation objectives, Israel favours more stringent restrictions than those under the 2015 nuclear deal, including permanently preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons; the removal of highly-enriched Uranium; comprehensive limits on enrichment; dismantling key nuclear facilities at Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow and intrusive monitoring.[17]
Israel maintains that any resolution should constrain Iran’s ballistic missiles and support for non-state allies, regarded as integral components of Iran’s broader security threat. For the Netanyahu government facing elections, a limited direct role enables it to provide intelligence support to the US while reducing wartime disruption to civilian life and the economy.[18] Lastly, a contained but adversarial Iran may serve the Israel–US axis by reinforcing Gulf states’ security dependencies and facilitating incremental normalisation with the Jewish state.[19]

articles.title: Qatar's Amir Says Hormuz Closure, Attacks on Gas Facilities Disrupt LNG Exports - Arab Times Kuwait News
