articles.full_text:
13/10/2026
DOHA, Oct 13: Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and direct damage to energy facilities in Ras Laffan had disrupted a significant share of the country’s exports, warning that the impact extended to global energy markets.
Addressing the Consultative Council, Sheikh Tamim said Qatar accounts for approximately one-fifth of global liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade, meaning disruptions to its exports could quickly affect international markets and consumers, Anadolu Agency reported.
He said the economic impact of the regional crisis had been concentrated mainly in the energy sector. QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March following drone attacks on energy facilities in Mesaieed and Ras Laffan, home to the world’s largest liquefied natural gas export hub.
Qatar’s Ministry of Defence said two drones, which it said originated from Iran, had targeted the facilities. The attacks caused damage to critical energy infrastructure, while the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz further affected Qatar’s ability to export its energy supplies.
Despite the setbacks, Sheikh Tamim said development of the North Field gas project was continuing according to plan, as Qatar seeks to increase its LNG production capacity. He also highlighted progress on the Golden Pass LNG project in the United States and said QatarEnergy was continuing to expand its international investments and partnerships.
On security, the Amir said Iran had attacked Qatar, describing the attacks as a violation of the country’s sovereignty and international law. He said Qatar’s armed forces and security services had fulfilled their responsibilities in protecting the state.
Sheikh Tamim stressed that Qatar’s pursuit of dialogue and a peaceful settlement did not mean compromising its national defence. He said the country’s strategy was to protect its sovereignty while avoiding being drawn into war, maintaining essential public services and supply chains, and sustaining economic activity.
He also called for efforts to facilitate a ceasefire, restore maritime navigation and support negotiations to resolve the regional crisis.
The emir urged Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states to strengthen coordination and cooperation, stressing the importance of protecting commercial shipping through the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as well as energy facilities, water infrastructure and civilian installations.
His remarks underscored Qatar’s concerns over the combined impact of regional hostilities, damage to energy infrastructure and restrictions on a vital international shipping route on the country’s economy and global LNG supplies.

articles.title: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize - The Dispatch
articles.summary: Why Hamas Cheered Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize  The DispatchPillay decries US sanctions on ICC, where she is ‘confident’ Netanyahu will one day stand trial  The Times of IsraelTrump swipes at Nobel committee after peace prize awarded to human rights lawyer  PoliticoMy relative defined ‘genocide.’ Honoring him means scrutinizing Navi Pillay’s Israel findings.  Jewish Telegraphic AgencyAnalysing Africa newsletter: A Nobel and ignoble day for the rule of l...
articles.full_text:
It’s not every day that an Islamist death cult celebrates the announcement of the Nobel Peace Prize winner, but that is exactly what happened on Friday evening when Hamas welcomed the selection of Navi Pillay as “an important step toward international justice.” Why is Oslo’s humanitarian hero winning applause from an Iranian-backed terror proxy that massacred families and kidnapped children?
I have dealt with Pillay in Geneva since she arrived here in 2008 as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights. Over 18 years, I watched her turn the language of universal rights into a weapon aimed relentlessly at the Jewish state.
It began with a welcome. In September 2008, my team at U.N. Watch publicly saluted her struggle against South African apartheid. Her story deserved respect. But already then, her first act as U.N. human rights chief was to champion Durban II, the planned Geneva follow-up to the notorious 2001 conference in South Africa, where an ostensible campaign against racism became a festival of antisemitism.
At Durban I, thousands of radical activists marched against Israel and Jews, some carrying signs praising Adolf Hitler. Jewish students were threatened. The Arab Lawyers Union handed out cartoons of hook-nosed Jews. Copies of The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, the notorious antisemitic forgery, were openly distributed. At the NGO Forum, Israel was declared a “racist apartheid state” and accused of “genocide.” In the Durban outcome document, the Jewish state alone was singled out as a perpetrator of racism. Rep. Tom Lantos, a Holocaust survivor, called it “the most sickening and unabashed display of hate for Jews” he had witnessed since the Nazi era.
Pillay wanted to rehabilitate Durban. We wanted to prevent a repeat. Alarm bells started ringing when Muammar Gaddafi’s Libyan regime was appointed chair of the preparatory committee, and Iran the vice chair.
Months before the April 2009 conference, Pillay was already rebuking the U.S., Canada, and Israel for threatening to boycott, dismissing their “all or nothing” approach, and warning against “pretexts for inaction.” In the end, Canada, Italy, the U.S., Germany, Australia, and the Netherlands were among 10 countries that boycotted.
When Durban II finally opened, Holocaust denier Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, then president of Iran, was the first head of state to speak. He used the Geneva podium to denounce Israel’s existence. France, along with many other European delegations, walked out of the room in protest. Pillay defended Ahmadinejad’s right to speak, and urged against more countries pulling out of the conference.
That same year, after Hamas and Israel fought a three-week war, the U.N. Human Rights Council condemned Israel and created a commission of inquiry. Pillay recruited Richard Goldstone to serve as chair, with her staff doing most of the work. The inquiry’s September 2009 report was a bombshell, accusing Israel’s political and military leaders of a “deliberately disproportionate attack designed to punish, humiliate and terrorize a civilian population.” It called for action by the International Criminal Court, and for criminal proceedings in foreign courts under universal jurisdiction.
The report was a travesty of justice. A year and a half later, in a Washington Post op-ed, Goldstone himself retracted the core charge.
It later emerged that Pillay’s office had hired Grietje Baars, a radical Marxist law professor, to write key sections of the report. Before joining the investigation, Baars had already described Israel’s operation as a “massacre.” While working on it, Baars signed a declaration denouncing Israel’s “apartheid regime.” The next year, in 2010, Baars joined the Hamas-backed Gaza flotilla campaign as a European spokesman.
Under Pillay’s leadership, this is what passed for fact-finding at the U.N. I later submitted a legal complaint to the secretary-general about Pillay’s hiring of Baars. I received no reply.
Pillay herself “strongly condemned” Israel’s use of force as “disproportionate” as soon as the fighting began. Her verdict preceded the examination. By contrast, joining the U.S. and Canada, German Chancellor Angela Merkel stated that Israel had a right to self-defense and that responsibility for the conflict lay “clearly and exclusively” with Hamas. Even U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs John Holmes spoke out against “the reckless and cynical use of civilian installations by Hamas.” Not Pillay.
In January 2009, after years of rocket attacks from Gaza, Israel imposed a naval blockade to prevent weapons reaching Hamas by sea. In May 2010, Turkey’s terrorist-linked IHH organized a flotilla which set out to breach it. When Israeli commandos boarded its lead ship, the Mavi Marmara, they were attacked by militants wielding iron bars, clubs, chains, and slingshots.
Within hours, Pillay declared that Israel treated international law with “perpetual disdain,” denouncing the blockade as “inhumane and illegal.” Yet the subsequent Palmer inquiry appointed by the U.N. secretary-general concluded that the naval blockade was lawful—a legitimate security measure to prevent weapons from entering Gaza by sea. Again, Pillay’s verdict came before she examined the facts—or the law.
By 2014, Pillay had endorsed the charge that when Palestinian men beat their wives, it’s Israel’s fault. “Women with husbands explained that the dire economic situation and the pressures of the occupation have made men more violent because they have lost their ability to provide and protect — two essential elements of manhood in a traditional patriarchal society,” Special Rapporteur Yakin Ertürk wrote in 2005, following her visit to Palestinian territories. “As men become stripped of their manhood, women become the shock absorbers of the crises as targets of domestic violence.” Nine years later, Pillay reported to the U.N. that this analysis “remains valid.”
After leaving the U.N. human rights office in 2014, Pillay dropped any pretense of distance. In 2020, she signed a campaign titled “Sanction Apartheid Israel!” In June 2021, she joined a letter blaming Israeli “domination and oppression” for the previous month’s war, which began with Hamas firing rockets at Jerusalem and other Israeli cities.
A month later, the president of the Human Rights Council—Nazhat Shameem Khan, now a deputy prosecutor of the International Criminal Court—appointed Pillay to chair an inquiry into the very conflict for which she had already blamed Israel. But its mandate went even further: a permanent investigation of alleged violations before and after the 2021 clash, reaching into the conflict’s “underlying root causes,” with no end date. The campaigner became the investigator, and Pillay’s verdict came with her appointment.
In February 2022, U.N. Watch submitted a detailed legal brief requesting Pillay’s recusal. We cited her statements and the U.N.’s own impartiality standards. We received no reply.
That June, I walked up to Pillay at the Human Rights Council and handed her a copy. She acknowledged having seen our motion.
“We never received a reply,” I said.
“We can’t respond to everything,” she answered.
Everything? This was a core challenge to her fitness to preside. A few days ago, Pillay claimed that her inquiry “essentially worked like a court.” Yet a judge cannot dismiss a recusal motion as unwanted correspondence.
Later, in July 2022, her fellow commissioner Miloon Kothari railed against “the Jewish lobby” and questioned Israel’s U.N. membership. Pillay defended him, claiming his remarks had been taken out of context. In the end, Kothari retracted his comments after numerous democracies condemned him for antisemitism, as did the Human Rights Council chair himself. Pillay never recanted.
In September 2025, the Pillay inquiry fulfilled its purpose: It accused Israel of genocide. The report was built on selective quotations used to infer genocidal intent, and a complete sidelining of Hamas’ military infrastructure and use of civilian sites. According to the Pillay report’s chronology, it was Israel that attacked on October 7.
Pillay’s accusation of genocide against Israel appears to be what prompted the Nobel. Her earlier achievements—as a judge in South Africa and on the U.N.’s Rwanda tribunal—were known for decades. That record deserves recognition. But it also makes her disregard for impartiality harder to excuse.
She knew the standards. A reputation earned in one courtroom cannot exempt its owner from scrutiny in another. Nor can past courage transform a partisan investigation into justice simply because its findings carry the United Nations seal.
Pillay was named to the inquiry for her authority as a judge, but she acted on the commitments of a campaigner. The Nobel Committee is now seeking to magnify her imprimatur.
Hamas understands the benefit perfectly. Its war against Israel gains a prestigious legal vocabulary, and its victims recede behind an indictment of the state that defended them. That is why Hamas cheered. The Nobel Committee should now tell the world whether this is its desired outcome.

articles.title: Blasts rock Saudi cities as Yemen conflict escalates
articles.summary: Loud explosions were reported in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and near state oil giant Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran on Tuesday, as escalating hostilities with Yemen's...
articles.full_text:
Loud explosions were reported in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and near state oil giant Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran on Tuesday, as escalating hostilities with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis fueled fears of a wider regional confrontation.
Six sources told Reuters that explosions were heard near Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, which had been evacuated. One source reported seeing smoke rising from the facility, although the company had not issued an official statement confirming an attack or damage.
In Riyadh, a powerful blast was heard shortly after Saudi civil defense authorities warned residents of an incoming aerial threat.
"The city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat," an emergency alert sent to residents said.
The incidents followed threats by the Houthis to retaliate against Saudi airstrikes targeting rebel-held areas of Yemen.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition carried out fresh strikes on the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, according to the rebel-run Al Masirah broadcaster and local residents.
Witnesses reported powerful explosions hours after coalition aircraft targeted the al-Suhaba fuel facility west of the city.
The coalition had previously urged civilians to evacuate the Yemeni Oil Company facility and nearby storage areas ahead of possible strikes.
The company, however, said its storage facilities were empty and insisted that any attack would not disrupt fuel supplies. Despite those assurances, residents reported long lines at gas stations amid fears of shortages.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned that further Saudi strikes on Sanaa would trigger a "firm and painful" response against Riyadh.
The renewed violence follows a series of deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi authorities are investigating how their air defenses failed to intercept the missiles and drones used in the attacks.
The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday that its forces had intercepted three drones north of Riyadh, although the claim could not be independently verified.
The latest escalation comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces battle the Houthis for control of strategic territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping corridor connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Fighting intensified last month after Houthi forces seized key positions overlooking the waterway, prompting a Saudi-backed offensive to regain control.
Saudi Arabia's Cabinet warned Tuesday that the Houthis would face consequences for continued attacks on the kingdom.
"The Kingdom will not allow any threat to its security or to freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait," the Cabinet said in a statement carried by Saudi state television.
Meanwhile, Yemen's Interior Ministry said Houthi attacks on the southwestern city of Taiz had killed six people and wounded 18 over the previous 24 hours.
A commander with Saudi-backed government forces said Houthi fighters had reached the outskirts of Taiz, with some entering the city despite fierce resistance.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the commander said the rebels had deployed substantial forces supported by short- and medium-range ballistic missiles.
He identified the Kahboub mountains, which overlook the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the southern port city of Aden, as a critical battleground, adding that government forces had requested reinforcements.
The widening confrontation has disrupted regional aviation and raised concerns over commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime routes.
The Houthis renewed warnings Tuesday against using Saudi airspace, while several airlines have suspended flights to the kingdom following attacks on airports.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty condemned the attacks during a phone call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, urging the Houthis to immediately halt strikes against Saudi Arabia.
"There is no justification for these attacks, and they cannot be accepted," Abdelatty said, according to an Egyptian statement.
He also called for renewed diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict between Iran and the United States and prevent further regional instability.
Washington has provided Saudi Arabia with intelligence, targeting assistance and military planning support but has so far refrained from directly striking Houthi positions.
Saudi Arabia has sought greater U.S. military involvement as the fighting intensifies, although analysts warn that direct American intervention could prompt the Houthis to further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The latest developments underscore growing concerns that the conflict in Yemen could expand into a broader regional confrontation, threatening energy infrastructure, civilian aviation and international trade.

articles.title: Houthi rebels report airstrikes in Yemen, and other Middle East developments - The Standard-Speaker
articles.summary: Houthi rebels report airstrikes in Yemen, and other Middle East developments  The Standard-Speaker
articles.full_text:
By The Associated Press
Iran appears to be targeting vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers around the Strait of Hormuz, according to a military institute. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched new airstrikes on Tuesday on Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and residents.
The strikes followed a coalition spokesman’s warning urging residents to evacuate the area. A spokesman for the Iran-backed rebels warned that any attack on Sanaa would draw a “harsh and painful” response against the Saudi capital.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.
Ship-to-ship oil transfers at risk, military institute says
Iran appears to be targeting commercial vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in and near the Strait of Hormuz in order to try to undermine vessels’ ability to move energy through the strait, the Institute for the Study of War said Tuesday.
Iran may be developing its anti-ship missile capabilities, the U.S.-based think tank said in a post on X.
The U.K.’s Maritime Trade Operations Centre posted on X Monday that at least three vessels had been attacked by unknown projectiles in the strait a day earlier. There were no immediate claims of responsibility.
But Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s top security body, told state TV on Saturday that Iranian forces were striking an average of five “smuggling ships” every night.
Rezaei appeared to be referring to U.S. efforts to guide oil shipments through the strait before the oil is transferred to larger tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman.
Iran demands evidence from U.K. on alleged airbase plot
Iran told British Ambassador Hugo Shorter on Tuesday that it could “seriously reconsider” bilateral relations unless the U.K. provides evidence linking Tehran to an alleged plot at the U.S.-run military air base RAF Fairford, Iran’s state broadcaster reported.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.
The Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, said the ambassador was informed of Tehran’s protest over what it called Britain’s “irresponsible and destructive approach.”
“The British government must provide documents and evidence supporting its accusations against Iran,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said.
The move came as MI5 chief Ken McCallum said Tuesday that Iran was seeking to target military sites in Britain and that the suspected September plot at RAF Fairford was “not unique.”
McCallum, who leads the U.K.’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond its traditional targets, Iranian opponents of the Islamic authorities. That has included arson attacks on Jewish sites that Britain says were carried out by Iranian proxies.
Police have arrested seven men in the investigation into the alleged plot on the airbase, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran, but all have been released on bail and no one has been charged.
Israel raids civil society offices in West Bank
Dozens of Israeli soldiers spilled from armored vehicles onto the streets of the West Bank city of Ramallah on Tuesday, raiding the offices of Palestinian charities and civil society organizations that Israel has long suspected of maintaining ties to militants and political factions.
The Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees and Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association were both among the groups targeted, officials with the organizations said. Soldiers could be seen carrying files from one office, and they fired tear gas to disperse Palestinian journalists filming them.
Ramallah is the administrative capital of the Palestinian Authority, and the raids underscored its shrinking autonomy under Israeli occupation, despite being the internationally recognized government of the occupied territory. The Palestinian Health Ministry reported two injuries, including a 14-year-old boy wounded in the upper thigh by Israeli gunfire. Several other people were treated for tear gas inhalation, the ministry said. The Israeli military did not respond to questions about the raid.
Farther north in the occupied territory, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israeli troops would remain in the Tulkarem refugee camp and rejected calls to allow its residents to return. Palestinians fled the camp in 2025 as the Israeli military carried out a widespread crackdown against West Bank militants.
“These are not residents, these are terrorists,” Netanyahu said in a video released Tuesday by his office during a visit to the nearby camp.
Saudi-led coalition strikes Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital
The Saudi-led coalition carried out new airstrikes Tuesday on Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and local residents.
The strikes came shortly after a coalition spokesman urged residents to evacuate the area for their safety. Witnesses in Sanaa reported hearing explosions, but it was not immediately clear what was hit.
Earlier, Gen. Yahya Saree, a spokesman for the Iran-backed rebels, warned that any attack on Sanaa would draw a “harsh and painful” response against the Saudi capital.
The exchange of threats comes as Saudi Arabiainvestigates why its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. An attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Trump declines to say if he’ll endorse anyone in Israeli election
Two weeks out from Israeli national elections, U.S. President Donald Trump again declined to say if he would endorse a candidate.
“We haven’t even thought about it,” he said. “Well, we may, I may be doing something,” he added, but provided no details.
The elections are the first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack, and the war in Gaza. The outcome threatens to end the career of Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. He is the only senior figure from Oct. 7 still in power, making the Oct. 27 election in many ways a referendum on his leadership.
Trump sidestepped a question earlier this month on Netanyahu’s reelection bid. The lack of an endorsement is a setback for the Israeli leader, who has touted his close relationship with Trump as one reason voters should choose him to once again lead the governing coalition.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

articles.title: Trump Considers Re-attacking Houthis after Earlier ‘Half-Measures’ Leave Job Unfinished - The Washington Stand

articles.full_text:
As the U.S. midterms inch ever closer, American fuel prices remain stratospheric because events in the Middle East remain far from settled. The Iranian regime’s strongest remaining proxy group has now taken the lead in sowing chaos and destruction across the region, with a particular focus on Saudi oil production. Conditions are so concerning that even France is sending troops to defend its interests. President Donald Trump has also said he is considering re-entering the conflict he left more than a year earlier.
On “Washington Watch,” Dr. Michael Rubin, director of Policy Analysis at the Middle East Forum, called the situation “déjà vu all over again.” Upon taking office, President Trump re-designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organization and in March 2025 ordered combat operations against them, which ultimately lasted for 51 days.
The catalyst for the conflict was the October 7 terror attack on Israel. As part of the Iranian terror network’s multi-front assault on Israel, the Houthis not only lobbed the occasional missile, but they exploited their strategic position along the Red Sea to once again target passing cargo ships. By June 2024, the U.S. Navy was responding to “near-daily” attacks by the Houthis in what the Associated Press called “the most intense running sea battle the Navy has faced since World War II.”
American operations successfully destroyed most of the Houthis’ military capabilities. But then, in May 2025, the Trump administration negotiated a separate ceasefire with the Houthis, which ignored their attack on Israel and ignored their close ties to Iran. Effectively, after running out of bombing targets, the U.S. left the region with the job half-finished, hoping it could call the ceasefire a victory. In many ways, this partial failure prefigured the 2026 conflict with Iran.
One reason the U.S. strategy suffered was that it lacked any coordination with other players in the region, such as other groups battling the Houthis for control of Yemen. “The southern forces who were resisting the Houthis said they didn’t have warning when Donald Trump began this campaign, and they didn’t have warning 51 days later when he stopped bombing,” Rubin recalled. “If there had been any coordination, maybe … the Anti-Houthi factions [would have] taken the port of Mocha, which is on the strategic choke point, the Bab Al-Mandeb.”
As it happened, the Houthis seized control of the critical port “because the people who used to defend that were people [who] were trained by the United Arab Emirates,” Rubin explained, and Saudi “Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman … put his own personal rivalry with the Emirates above common sense,” ordering airstrikes against the anti-Houthi faction.
Currently, the Houthis have never “had it so good,” Rubin added. “They never expected that they would be able to take the port of Mocha on the Bab Al-Mandeb. … From the Iranian perspective, from the Pakistani-Iranian border to the Bab Al-Mandeb on the Red Sea, that’s about 1,600 miles of coastline they, more or less effectively, control.”
This geographic connection is part of what makes the Houthis Iran’s strongest proxy. Whereas Hamas in Gaza is effectively cut off from Iran, and Hezbollah in Lebanon relies on weapons smuggled over land through Syria and Iraq, the Houthis in Yemen have direct maritime access. In fact, “the Houthis … resupply in three ways,” Rubin explained. “One is by sea, primarily through the port of Hudaydah. The second is by air through Sana’a International Airport, which the Houthis now control, and the third is overland from the Sultanate of Oman.”
This means that, although the U.S. heavily bombed the Houthis just last year, the terror group has already been able to rebuild its capacity significantly.
Another strength of the Houthis is their historic connection to northern Yemen. “They’re not simply an Iranian proxy,” said Rubin. “About 60 or 70 years ago, the Houthis — or their ancestors, I should say — ran Yemen. They had a Shiite imamate in Yemen. So, when you talk to Yemenis, what they say is, ‘We don’t like the Houthis. They’ve been co-opted by the Iranians, but they are Yemenis. They’re going to stay here even if Iran’s regime collapses.’” That deters dissatisfied Yemenis from undermining the Houthi cause, knowing that any resistance could be used against them later.
“Meanwhile, fighting has intensified between Saudi-led forces in Yemen and the Iran-backed Houthis terrorist group,” Perkins noted. The Houthis have attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh 20 times this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333. They have also attacked Saudi oil refineries, pipelines, and facilit[ies] they claimed was a “Saudi military operations HQ.”
Such firepower makes the terrorists bold. The Houthis reacted to the news that America may re-engage combat operations against them by threatening a “swift and painful response.” “I don’t know what to make of that,” Perkins responded; the Houthis must understand that the U.S. military is far stronger and more capable.
Unfortunately, Americans have often lacked the will to treat the Houthis with the firmness they require, Rubin admitted. “Barack Obama made a deal with the Saudis when the Houthis took over Sana’a, that the United States was going to help the Saudis with intelligence and help refuel Saudi planes as they bomb the Houthis. And then, of course, the progressive wing started complaining, and Barack Obama stopped doing that,” he said. “Ditto with Joe Biden. … When there was talk, for example, of cutting off this port of Hudaydah … Joe Biden listened to Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and others who said, ‘You can’t do this because then people might actually go hungry for three or four days until the fight is over.’”
America’s lack of willpower influenced the decisions of our would-be allies. “If the United States wasn’t serious about defeating the Houthis, and if we were going to cave in to progressive pressure, then what the Saudis were going to do instead of defeating the Houthis was co-opt them,” Rubin described. “Basically, the Saudis and the Houthis struck a bargain for quiet, in exchange for an end [to] Saudi bombing.”
“The problem is, when you co-opt Islamic ideologues, they will always stab you in the back,” Rubin added. “The Saudis are learning this lesson with the Houthis. You got to stop playing footsie with these guys and just defeat them.”
The U.S. government could stand to learn the same lesson. Unfortunately, “because we have a separation of church and state in the United States, too many of our policy makers in the State Department, even in the Central Intelligence Agency, look at religion as a third rail they can’t touch, and they don’t understand how it can be a motivating factor, especially among Islamists,” Rubin lamented.
Indeed, America should keep this principle in mind when dealing with just about every Muslim power in the Middle East, even the ones who currently pose as our friends. Rubin pointed out that the Saudis have their ideological version of Islam, but “the difference is that the Iranians have been exporting it much more.” He pointed to an ominous new defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. “Each of those states — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey — want to lead the Islamic world. … Those states that we’ve been counting on as allies for so long don’t have our best interests at heart. … Each of these three states is closer now to China than they are to the United States.”
While considering operations against the Houthis, the president has also said, regarding Iran, “that there will be no major military strikes between now and after the midterm elections,” Perkins observed. “We’ve seen this ‘on again, off again’ before. And it’s only led to Iran kind of regrouping and regaining strength” — just like with the Houthis.
After nearly obliterating the Iranian regime’s armed forces and senior leadership earlier this year, “now I’m trying to be nice. I want to be a nice person,” Trump said. Indeed, he regretted eliminating so many of Iran’s leaders, because that left so few potential parties with whom he can negotiate. “I should have probably left the leaders because I don’t know who we’re negotiating with,” the president reflected.
“There has not been any significant movement on the diplomatic front. Part of the problem is we really still don’t know who exactly is in charge inside Iran,” Rubin affirmed. “The Iranians keep trying to impeach the various cabinet ministers. It’s a big fight among the various factions … each more hardliner than the last.”
However, Rubin would amend Trump’s regretful musings. “There’s always been factions in Iran,” he said. “Part of the problem was our strategy. What President Donald Trump should have done is make an offer that Iranians couldn’t refuse; if they did refuse, then that person is removed from the battlefield, and you go on to the next one.”
“For example, Donald Trump was trying to negotiate with the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf,” he said. “What you need to do is systematically eliminate all the other factions. If you don’t, then ultimately, you’re starting from scratch.”
“Certainly President Donald Trump is right that the sea blockade has been working,” Rubin agreed. “As the United States and international partners have cut off Iran’s ability to export oil and import gasoline, the land borders of Iran —especially in the north, with Turkey, with Azerbaijan, with Turkmenistan — have flooded open. So, in a way, the Iranians have been able to resupply over land. I’m not sure we’ve been doing enough to actually stem that flow.”
The fundamental challenge here is that “Iran is a huge country,” he said. “It’s about six times the size of Great Britain. And, the fact of the matter is, it’s going to take a lot more than simply a maritime blockade to grind them into concession.”

articles.title: As Trump Weighs Joining War on Houthis, A Throwback To Yemen Bombing That Shook U.S. Navy! - EurAsian Times
articles.summary: As Trump Weighs Joining War on Houthis, A Throwback To Yemen Bombing That Shook U.S. Navy!  EurAsian Times
articles.full_text:
Barely weeks after rejecting Saudi Arabia’s request to join the air campaign against the Houthi rebels in Yemen, US President Donald Trump is rethinking his decision and has suggested that he may join the war against the Iran-backed Houthis.
The latest Houthi strikes on Saudi targets have revived a long-running American dilemma in Yemen — one that stretches back to the October 2000 bombing of the US Navy warship, which killed 17 U.S. sailors.
At least 25 people have been killed in Houthi drone and missile strikes on Saudi Arabia’s airports in recent weeks.
Separately, Houthis have occupied key port cities on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, threatening to choke the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, another key oil shipping route in the Middle East.
The rising Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key US ally in the Middle East, the threat of choking another global oil-supply route ahead of the US midterm elections, and the death of an American citizen have created a dilemma for President Trump on whether to open a new front in the Middle East.
Following the strike on Riyadh airport, Trump suggested that the US might join the Saudi war against the Houthis. “We may. We’re gonna look at it … We’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” Trump replied on October 12 when asked whether Washington is considering joining the Saudi War against the Houthis.
Notably, last month Trump rejected the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s request to join the Kingdom’s war against the Houthis.
However, the decision to open a new front against the Houthis will not be an easy one, as Trump realizes that the war in Yemen could become another quagmire for the US when it is already tied down in the Iran War since February this year.
Operation Decisive Storm to Operation Rough Rider
Trump launched Operation Rough Rider against the Houthis in March 2025, barely two months after taking the oath in January last year. The U.S. launched a major air and naval campaign after the Houthis resumed Red Sea attacks following the breakdown of a Gaza ceasefire.
Over the course of the next three months, the US struck over 1000 targets in Yemen, including radar systems, air defenses, missile and drone launch sites, manufacturing facilities, and some leadership targets.
However, the US abruptly ended the campaign in May, after agreeing to an Oman-brokered ceasefire. Houthis agreed to stop attacking U.S. vessels; the US halted strikes.
Trump later described the deal as Houthis “capitulating” under pressure; however, analysts disagreed as the ceasefire agreement did not cover Israel, the country that participated with Washington in bombing Houthi targets.
A New York Times investigation later revealed that Trump agreed to the ceasefire as the costs of the war exceeded $1 billion in munitions alone.
The US also lost three F/A-18 Super Hornet fighter jets and more than 15 MQ-9 Reaper drones in the campaign; however, it did not substantially weaken the Houthi position in Yemen.
However, the US involvement with Yemen goes much further back.
The USS Cole Bombing in Yemen
The US’s two-decade-long ‘War on Terror’ began after the 9/11 al-Qaeda attacks in 2001.
However, that was not the first time that Osama bin Laden-led terrorist group had attacked Americans or U.S. interests.
Just one year earlier, on October 12, 2000, al-Qaeda carried out a suicide boat attack on the USS Cole, a US Navy guided-missile destroyer, while it was refueling in the port of Aden, Yemen.
The blast killed 17 American sailors and wounded nearly 40 others. It also tore a roughly 40-foot-wide hole in the ship’s hull near the waterline.
The crew’s damage-control efforts saved the vessel.
The US destroyer, en route to the Persian Gulf, was making a prearranged fuel stop at the port of Aden, Yemen, when the attack occurred.
Before al-Qaeda used civilian airliners to strike the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, it used a small inflatable boat as a suicide bomb to strike the US Navy destroyer.
In fact, the USS Cole bombing was al-Qaeda’s second attempt to target a US Navy vessel near a Yemeni port.
The investigation revealed that the USS Cole bombing followed an unsuccessful attempt on January 3, 2000, to bomb another US Navy ship, the USS The Sullivans.
In this earlier incident, the terrorist boat sank before the explosives could be detonated; however, the boat and the explosives were salvaged. The Navy refitted the boat, tested the explosives, and reused them in the USS Cole attack.
The extensive FBI investigation ultimately determined that members of the al Qaeda terrorist network planned and carried out the bombing.
By the end of 2000, Yemeni authorities had arrested several suspects, including Jamal Muhammad Ahmad Al-Badawi and Fahad Muhammad Ahmad Al-Quso, two of the alleged masterminds of the USS The Sullivans and the USS Cole plots.
Al-Badawi and Al-Quso, known al Qaeda operatives who trained in al Qaeda camps in Afghanistan during the 1990s, were later killed in separate U.S. airstrikes.
However, the US failed to anticipate that such suicide attacks could be replicated on a much grander scale by using aircraft to attack US buildings.
It also failed to infiltrate al-Qaeda ranks to uncover plans for further attacks on the US.
Less than a year after the USS Cole bombing, al-Qaeda struck again, this time on US soil, executing the deadliest terror attack inside the US in history.
The Cole attack was part of al-Qaeda’s escalating campaign against the US after the 1998 East Africa embassy bombings.
It demonstrated al-Qaeda’s ability to strike a major U.S. military target overseas and served as a powerful propaganda victory.
The 9/11 Commission Report noted that the USS Cole attack “galvanized al-Qaeda’s recruitment efforts.”
Bin Laden ordered a propaganda video featuring a reenactment of the blast, training-camp footage, and calls to jihad.
The 9/11 Commission Report also noted that the planning for both the USS Cole attack and the 9/11 attacks took place during al-Qaeda’s summit in Kuala Lumpur in January 2000.
In retrospect, it’s clear that the USS Cole bombing was al-Qaeda’s warning to the US that more such attacks are coming; however, Washington failed to read the warning.
Yemen, in fact, was a major base for al-Qaeda before the rise of the Ansar Allah movement (precursor to the Houthis) in the early 2000s.
Osama bin Laden’s family also came from Yemen’s Hadhramaut region, and he saw the country as strategically important because of its weak central authority, remote tribal areas, and geography.
Al-Qaeda in Yemen was also responsible for the 1992 Aden hotel bombings targeting hotels used by US Marines en route to Somalia.
Aden hotel bombings were one of the first al-Qaeda terrorist attacks against the US.
In the 1990s and early 2000s, it was al-Qaeda in Yemen, and now it’s the Houthis; Yemen has been serving as a base for anti-US activities in the Middle East for over three decades now.

Former U.S. President Barack Obama criticized Israel’s approach, warning that military superiority alone cannot deliver lasting security and that denying Palestinians meaningful concessions risks eroding Israel’s moral credibility.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay in Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should "pain everybody,” describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
"That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
"If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
"That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
"I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
"It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

The U.S. is considering using its largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran if President Donald Trump revives the dormant war, CNN reported Thursday.
The military plans to use the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, nicknamed the "Mother Of All Bombs," to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, the news outlet reported, quoting officials familiar with the matter.
Trump seeks to boost his low approval ratings ahead of November midterm elections, with polls showing the unpopular war in Iran and resulting fuel and other price increases are hurting his Republican Party.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, which erupted with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have stalled since the summer.
But officials doubt the bomb's efficacy if deployed, particularly its ability to destroy suspected underground nuclear sites in the Islamic republic.
"The MOAB is a massive information operations weapon that is effective for large-area clearance but not much else," a source familiar with the plans told CNN.
"It is not designed as a deep penetration warhead."
The U.S. and Israel said the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal Tehran has long denied pursuing.
Concerns also exist about potential civilian casualties from such a large weapon.
Washington has in recent weeks dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
In 2017, the U.S. military in Afghanistan dropped the MOAB to target Daesh hideouts in a complex of tunnels and bunkers, killing more than 90 terrorists.

articles.title: Hormuz crisis is testing the world’s trade routes — and the UAE’s strategy - Gulf News
articles.summary: Hormuz crisis is testing the world’s trade routes — and the UAE’s strategy  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
UAE says years of investment in alternative routes are being tested by the crisis
Dubai: The disruption around the Strait of Hormuz is exposing just how vulnerable global trade remains to a single chokepoint, with businesses now being forced to find costly alternatives as geopolitical tensions reshape shipping, energy and supply chains.
For the UAE, the crisis is also putting its long-running strategy of building alternative ports, logistics networks and trade corridors to a real-world test.
Fahad Al Gergawi, Undersecretary at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Trade, said the country had spent decades preparing for precisely the kind of disruption now confronting global supply chains.
“The UAE has adopted a model that is different from the region – that is preparedness,” Al Gergawi said.
But he acknowledged the scale of the current challenge. “No one is anywhere used to a war being in the region directly to us,” he said, adding that periods of stress force countries to “look at different things from a different perspective”.
The UAE’s response, he said, has been to avoid putting all its dependence on one route or one mode of transport.
“The model of Dubai in the early 80s adopted a multi-model system of supply chain logistics that support businesses, but also focus on services,” Al Gergawi said.
The approach now includes ports, airports, logistics infrastructure, trade agreements and alternative corridors, including the UAE’s eastern coast.
“It’s not one way that you look at things,” he said. “You have to make yourself, as a system, as a country, as a nation, prepared for taking such decisions in short time and quickly.”
Farid Belbouab, Group CEO of Gulftainer, said the current crisis had demonstrated why having an alternative route is not simply a strategic advantage but increasingly a necessity.
“Resilience is about building multiple routes,” he said.
The UAE’s Khorfakkan port provides one such option, allowing cargo to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. But Belbouab cautioned against assuming that simply having another port solves the problem.
“You cannot pour concrete at the speed of a crisis,” he said.
The challenge, he said, is building an entire ecosystem capable of moving cargo when established routes are disrupted. “The port itself is not the only solution,” Belbouab said. “It’s about a network of an ecosystem.”
That means connecting ports to logistics parks, industrial facilities, roads and other transport links so cargo can be rerouted quickly.
Karen Young, Senior Research Scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, offered a less reassuring picture of what that rerouting means for the wider global economy.
The current disruption is “rewiring and remapping” energy flows and trade routes, she said, but warned that the consequences would be particularly severe for weaker economies.
The market can find alternative ways to move goods, Young said, but that does not mean those alternatives will be cheap or reliable.
“The market will figure out ways to get things from place A to place B,” she said.
“But it doesn’t mean that the price stays the same or that the availability in different markets is consistent.”
Young said the crisis was demonstrating the importance of storage, alternative energy sources and the ability to switch between different fuels and transport systems. “This crisis is teaching us about volatility and about responsiveness,” she said.
The pressure is not limited to oil and gas.
Young said the disruption was slowing the movement of wider categories of goods across the region, with consequences for re-export markets stretching from Africa to the Middle East and North Africa and South Asia.
The cost of moving energy has also surged, she said, citing the increase in the daily cost of a journey between the Gulf and East Asia from around $40,000 to $1.3 million.
“These are the kind of changes that certainly are inflationary for all of our energy products,” she said.
The implication for Gulf economies is significant: alternative routes may reduce the risk of a complete supply-chain stoppage, but they do not eliminate higher freight costs, congestion or uncertainty.
Florence Gaub, Director of the Research Division at the NATO Defense College, said the crisis also showed why trade could no longer be separated from security.
“The two worlds that seem to be disconnected for the longest time, they are connected, and they will continue to be connected,” she said.
The Strait of Hormuz is one example of how a strategic security issue can quickly become a global trade problem.
Gaub said the world could increasingly move towards relationships where countries continue trading despite serious political disagreements.
“I think we’re probably going to have some, call it ‘liquid alliances’,” she said. “I like to call it ‘frenemies’, where you continue to trade, but you actually don’t get along on other things.”
For smaller economies, North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timcho Mucunski said the answer was not to retreat behind economic barriers.
“The nations that succeed in the next five, 10, 15, 20 years will not be the nations that build the largest walls, but the nations that build the most resilient bridges,” he said. But the underlying challenge remains: countries need resilience without sacrificing connectivity.
“Resilience in no way means isolation,” Mucunski said.
Al Gergawi made a similar argument for the UAE, saying trade itself could help create the relationships needed to navigate geopolitical uncertainty.
“Interest is what brings people together, and trade is the hardcore part of that,” he said.
He pointed to the UAE-led Future Investment and Trade Partnership, launched with Switzerland, Singapore and New Zealand, as an effort by like-minded economies to navigate rising protectionism rather than wait for the global trading system to stabilise.
“Waiting is not an option for us,” Al Gergawi said. That approach is being tested now.
The current crisis has shown that alternative infrastructure can provide a buffer, but it has also exposed the cost and complexity of replacing established routes when geopolitical tensions disrupt them.
For the UAE, the question is therefore no longer whether alternative corridors are useful. It is whether the infrastructure, partnerships and regulatory systems built before the crisis can keep trade moving when the next disruption arrives.

Israel’s economy has always punched above its weight, but the last eighteen months have redefined its global position. Foreign investment flows, currency fluctuations, and shifting trade alliances now dictate daily decisions in Tel Aviv boardrooms and Haifa tech parks alike. The connection between international capital markets and local business strategy grows tighter with every quarter. For entrepreneurs watching these shifts, understanding the global playbook is no longer optional. One service that helps navigate these cross-border complexities is Charmius Canada, which provides practical market entry support for Israeli firms expanding into North American consumer sectors. Their approach bridges the gap between local innovation and international execution.
The numbers tell a compelling story about this interdependence. Consider the Bank of Israel’s recent interventions to stabilize the shekel, or the way US Federal Reserve rate decisions ripple through Israeli mortgage markets within hours. Global liquidity directly impacts start-up valuations in Tel Aviv, while commodity price swings alter the cost structure of the country’s manufacturing base. Meanwhile, the rise of digital entertainment economies worldwide has created unexpected crossovers. Israeli software developers now build platforms for international digital entertainment providers, and local marketing firms specialize in customer retention strategies for overseas clients, including sophisticated promotional structures that drive user engagement.
Key facts: Market data that reshapes strategy
The following statistics highlight how deeply global forces penetrate Israel’s business ecosystem. Each figure represents a concrete shift that decision-makers must factor into their planning.
- The shekel appreciated 4.2% against the dollar in Q1 2026, directly squeezing export margins for electronics manufacturers.
- Foreign direct investment reached $29.8 billion in 2025, with 63% originating from US and European venture funds.
- Israeli tech exits totaled $14.5 billion in 2025, a 22% increase from the previous year, driven largely by cross-border acquisitions.
- The Bank of Israel raised interest rates to 4.75% in January 2026, tracking Federal Reserve policy to prevent capital outflow.
- Trade with Asian markets grew 31% year-over-year, with India and South Korea emerging as primary partners for cybersecurity solutions.
- Inflation-adjusted wages in the high-tech sector rose 8.3% in 2025, outpacing the national average by nearly three times.
- Over 40% of Israeli start-ups now incorporate in Delaware or Nevada before their Series A round, reflecting US market priorities.
Currency wars and the Start-up Nation
Exchange rate volatility creates both headaches and opportunities for Israeli founders. When the shekel strengthens, local salaries become expensive for foreign investors, often triggering hiring freezes or delayed expansion plans. Conversely, a weaker currency makes Israeli R&D remarkably affordable, attracting acquisition interest from multinational corporations. The correlation between US Treasury yields and Tel Aviv stock performance has never been tighter. Portfolio managers in New York now treat Israeli tech equities as a direct proxy for global risk appetite, meaning local companies face pressure from sentiment shifts that have nothing to do with their fundamentals.
This dynamic extends beyond traditional finance. The digital entertainment technology sector, particularly companies developing interactive consumer platforms, demonstrates the fusion of local talent with global consumer trends. Israeli studios develop sophisticated engagement features and reward-based systems for international operators, adapting their engineering skills to meet overseas regulatory frameworks. These projects generate substantial foreign currency revenue while exposing local developers to best practices in user experience and retention modeling. The result is a two-way street where global market demands shape Israeli product development, and Israeli innovation enhances international digital experiences.
Trade corridors and strategic realignment
Israel’s trade relationships have undergone a structural transformation since 2023. The Abraham Accords opened direct commercial routes with Gulf states, while simultaneous tensions with traditional European partners pushed diversification. Asian markets, particularly China and Japan, now absorb significant portions of Israeli agricultural exports and medical device production. This realignment carries profound implications for business planning. Logistics chains that once relied on Mediterranean ports now incorporate overland corridors through Jordan and Saudi Arabia, reducing transit times by nearly 40% for certain goods.
The technology sector mirrors this geographic shift. Indian conglomerates now co-develop defense and cyber systems with Israeli partners, while South Korean chaebols invest heavily in local battery and energy storage research. These partnerships create stable revenue streams that partially insulate Israeli firms from Western market downturns. However, they also introduce new compliance burdens. Companies managing cross-border data flows must navigate divergent privacy standards, and those handling payment systems face varying consumer protection expectations. Successful firms treat these challenges as product features rather than obstacles, building compliance tools that serve multiple jurisdictions simultaneously.
Consumer behavior and global entertainment trends
Domestic consumer patterns now reflect international cultural currents more than ever. Israeli consumers, long known for early technology adoption, increasingly mirror spending habits seen in North America and Western Europe. This convergence manifests clearly in digital entertainment spending. Online platforms offering interactive entertainment experiences have seen subscriber growth of 28% annually, with users responding positively to introductory promotions and loyalty programs that originated in overseas markets. Local payment processors have adapted accordingly, supporting instant transactions and cryptocurrency options that appeal to younger demographics.
Marketing professionals in Israel now study global campaign effectiveness data to predict local responses. Campaigns that succeed in Toronto or London often translate well to Tel Aviv, provided they account for cultural nuances around holidays and family structures. This cross-pollination extends to customer service expectations. Israeli consumers now demand the same response times and personalization levels that international brands deliver, forcing local businesses to upgrade their support infrastructure. The businesses that thrive treat these rising standards as opportunities to differentiate themselves rather than burdens to minimize.
Strategic outlook for 2026 and beyond
The integration of global markets into Israel’s business environment shows no signs of slowing. Companies that succeed in the coming years will maintain flexible currency hedging strategies, diversify their investor bases across multiple continents, and build products that address universal consumer needs rather than purely local ones. The most resilient organizations treat international market data as a core input for every strategic decision, from pricing to hiring to product roadmap development.
For entrepreneurs and established firms alike, the practical takeaway is clear: Build relationships with international partners early, invest in compliance capabilities before they become urgent, and study consumer behavior across multiple markets simultaneously. The global economy offers enormous upside for Israeli businesses willing to embrace its complexity. Those who wait for stability before acting will find themselves competing against more agile rivals who treated uncertainty as a permanent condition rather than a temporary challenge. The data from 2025 and early 2026 confirms this approach works. The only question is who will execute it faster.

articles.full_text:
Iran said monitoring teams found the unnamed vessel ablaze after it entered a prohibited zone with its tracking systems disabled, two days after the container ship GFS Pride sank following a fire and the cargo ship Cape Dao also went down after being struck by a projectile.
An oil tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after entering what Iran's navy described as a prohibited zone with its tracking systems disabled, Iranian state-run media reported, the second such incident in the area in 24 hours.
Iran's navy said monitoring teams patrolling the eastern sector of the Strait of Hormuz detected the tanker ablaze in the restricted area, according to a statement cited by the Mehr news agency.
The name, flag and crew condition of the vessel were not immediately known, nor was the cause of the fire.
On Wednesday, Iranian domestic media reported a fire on another tanker near the Strait of Hormuz after it also switched off its tracking equipment.
The incidents follow the sinking of two commercial vessels in the same waters in recent days. The container ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after catching fire. All 21 crew members were rescued.
The IRGC said the vessel struck a sea mine, while maritime sources cited an unidentified projectile.
The cargo ship Cape Dao, which had previously been struck by a projectile, also sank. One crew member was killed in the initial attack.
Videos circulating on social media appeared to show cargo including mobile phones and luxury goods floating in the water near the Strait of Hormuz, with people in small boats collecting items.
Multiple international media outlets published the footage, as well as separate footage of containers and debris in waters reportedly near the strait. Euronews could not independently verify its veracity.
US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US military operations in the region, had not commented on Thursday's incident as of publication.
Tehran's expanded ban in place?
Iran's IRGC declared the waters leading to the Strait of Hormuz a prohibited zone in September, following remarks by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohbi said the zone covered part of the Gulf of Oman and part of the Arabian Sea along the approach to the strait.
Ali Azmayi, commander of the IRGC naval force, said Tehran exercises "smart control" over the strait and that all vessels seeking to transit the route must obtain permission, in response to US statements that the waterway remains open and under Washington's control.
Tehran has said vessels violating the rules in the area face penalties. Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed in late February at the start of the war with the US, which Washington followed up with its own naval blockade of the key waterway.

articles.title: Georgia seeks to strengthen trade ties with UAE - Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi
articles.summary: Georgia seeks to strengthen trade ties with UAE  Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi

Georgia intends to deepen economic ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and strengthen its transit capacity as competition grows over transport routes linking Central Asia and Europe.
Georgia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili presented the country’s transit potential at the Raisina Middle East conference in Abu Dhabi. She discussed opportunities to expand economic cooperation with the UAE and develop the Middle Corridor.
Speaking at a panel discussion titled “Resilience, partnership and the road ahead: the strategic future of the Gulf region,” Bochorishvili said Georgia has 16 free trade agreements, including deals with the European Union, China and the UAE.
She said the country’s strategic location and trade partnerships create broad opportunities for regional cooperation. Georgia’s ties with the UAE extend beyond bilateral relations.
UAE investment strengthens Middle Corridor links
Bochorishvili described Georgia as a key gateway connecting Central Asia with Europe and global markets. She identified stronger east-west transport links as one of the priorities for future cooperation.
The Middle Corridor runs from China and Central Asia across the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan and Georgia, and then reaches Europe via the Black Sea. Its importance has grown as countries seek to diversify trade routes and strengthen links between Asian and European markets.
The UAE already plays a significant role in Georgia’s logistics sector. Abu Dhabi-based AD Ports Group owns 60% of Tbilisi Dry Port. The rail-connected logistics facility links Georgia’s railway network with Black Sea ports. The project is part of efforts to improve cargo transportation along the Middle Corridor and expand trade.
Economic ties have also been strengthened by the Georgia-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, which entered into force in June 2024. The agreement aims to increase annual non-oil trade between the two countries from $481 million to $1.5 billion within five years.
Georgia calls for investment in transport infrastructure
Bochorishvili said Georgia, Azerbaijan and Türkiye had already laid the groundwork for developing regional connectivity through major transport and energy projects. She also noted that conflicts following the collapse of the Soviet Union had prevented the South Caucasus from fully realizing its potential as a regional transport hub.
The Foreign Minister called for greater investment in infrastructure, diversified economic partnerships and stronger cooperation based on trust. She stressed that excessive dependence on individual partners could undermine long-term economic resilience.
Despite its strategic location and broad network of trade agreements, Georgia faces challenges in turning its geographic advantages into a competitive international transit network. Its long-term success will depend on expanding transport capacity, improving logistics efficiency and ensuring reliable links across regional infrastructure.
Bochorishvili’s remarks in Abu Dhabi underscored Georgia’s intention to strengthen its role as a key link between Central Asia, the Gulf region and Europe, with the Middle Corridor central to that strategy.

articles.title: The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs is in defense tech - opinion - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs is in defense tech - opinion  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
For decades, Israel's technology story has been defined by its ability to turn military experience into commercial innovation. Cybersecurity is perhaps the clearest example. Young Israelis left elite military units with technological expertise, identified problems that extended far beyond the battlefield, and built companies that became global leaders.
Today, we are witnessing the beginning of another shift. Some of Israel's most ambitious entrepreneurs are no longer looking only to cybersecurity, enterprise software, or consumer technology for their next venture. Increasingly, they are choosing defense tech.
This is not simply a consequence of October 7, nor is it a temporary response to war. It reflects a broader transformation in the global technology industry and in how the next generation of Israeli entrepreneurs thinks about the problems worth solving.
From cyber to the battlefield
Five or 10 years ago, launching a defense start-up was far from an obvious choice for an Israeli entrepreneur. Defense markets were considered difficult to enter. Procurement cycles were long, customers were governments, regulation was complex, and venture capital investors often preferred the scalability and speed of software businesses. Many talented engineers and military veterans naturally gravitated toward cybersecurity, cloud computing, and enterprise software instead.
That calculation is changing.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed new technological needs at extraordinary speed. At the same time, rising geopolitical tensions have pushed governments across Europe, the United States, and elsewhere to rethink defense spending and technological preparedness.
The result is a market that looks very different from the one entrepreneurs faced only a few years ago.
But perhaps the most important change is not the amount of capital entering the sector. It is the people entering it. We are seeing entrepreneurs and early employees who combine operational military experience with backgrounds in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, software, and other areas that historically sat outside the traditional defense industry. We are also seeing experienced executives from Israel's defense companies who have spent years managing complex technological programs choose to build their own companies. This combination is particularly powerful.
Israel's unique advantage
Defense technology is different from conventional software. Understanding the technology is not enough. Founders need to understand how a product will actually be used under operational conditions, how military customers think, and what problems genuinely need to be solved.
Israel has an unusually deep pool of people with exactly that experience.
At the same time, it has one of the world's most mature start-up ecosystems. Engineers and entrepreneurs who understand AI, cloud infrastructure, and software can work alongside people who have spent years dealing with operational challenges in the field.
The convergence of these two worlds is difficult to replicate elsewhere.
Because it is already influencing the technologies being developed. Autonomous systems, counter-drone technologies, advanced sensing, cutting-edge artificial intelligence, and new forms of maritime and aerial defense are increasingly being approached with the speed and mindset of the technology industry rather than solely through traditional defense development cycles.
That distinction matters. The technological requirements of modern warfare are evolving too quickly for innovation to take years.
The start-up model enters defense
The traditional defense industry will remain essential. Building complex military platforms at scale requires enormous engineering, manufacturing, and integration capabilities.
Start-ups serve a different role.
They can focus on a single problem, experiment quickly, take technological risks, and adapt their products as operational needs evolve. The most interesting question, therefore, is not whether start-ups will replace traditional defense companies. They will not.
The question is what becomes possible when start-up speed is combined with the capabilities of established defense industries and the needs of military customers.
This is also why international collaboration will become increasingly important. No Israeli defense tech start-up should be built with Israel as its only market.
The challenges these companies are addressing are global. European countries are increasing defense investment, the United States is looking for ways to accelerate defense innovation, and militaries around the world are confronting many of the same challenges.
For Israeli entrepreneurs, the opportunity is therefore significantly larger than the domestic market. Building relationships with international investors, defense companies, governments, and military customers early will be critical to creating the next generation of global companies.
A new generation of Israeli technology companies
Israel has reinvented its technology ecosystem before.
The country's cybersecurity industry did not become a global powerhouse overnight. It emerged because a unique concentration of talent, experience, capital, and market demand came together at the right moment.
Defense tech may now be approaching a similar moment. There is capital entering the sector. There is global demand. Technological breakthroughs in AI, autonomy, robotics, and sensing are changing what is possible. Most importantly, a generation of Israeli entrepreneurs increasingly sees defense not as an old industry, but as one of the most consequential technological challenges of their careers.
For many of them, the motivation also differs from previous startup cycles. Recent events have made the problems they are trying to solve tangible and immediate. Building technology that protects soldiers, civilians and critical infrastructure is no longer an abstract market opportunity.
That sense of purpose should not be underestimated.
The next great Israeli technology company may still be a cybersecurity company, a fintech platform or an enterprise software business. Israel will continue to produce all of them.
But when we look at where some of the country's most ambitious engineers, experienced executives and returning entrepreneurs are choosing to spend the next decade of their lives, a new direction is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
The next generation of Israeli entrepreneurship is already taking shape. A significant part of it will be built in defense tech.
The author is a founding partner of Kinetica Ventures and an experienced investor in defense tech and cybersecurity, with a background spanning venture capital and the US Department of Defense.
