An Israeli airstrike on a Gaza City residential building killed a Palestinian woman and injured two others, including a girl, early Wednesday, according to sources.
A medical source at Al-Shifa Hospital told Türkiye's Anadolu Agency (AA) that the body of Reem Asaad Awad, 33, and two injured were brought to the hospital following the airstrike on a residential building in the Rimal neighborhood.
The source said the strike caused extensive destruction to the targeted apartment and neighboring buildings. A large fire also broke out after the attack and was later extinguished by civil defense crews.
Meanwhile, witnesses said Israeli military vehicles and quadcopter drones opened heavy fire toward Palestinian homes in the Tuffah neighborhood, northeast of Gaza City, while explosive devices were dropped on al-Sikka Street in the surrounding area.
Separately, sources said the Israeli army carried out a large-scale demolition operation, blowing up homes within areas where its forces are deployed east of Gaza City.
In the central Gaza Strip, witnesses said an incursion by Israeli military vehicles and bulldozers beyond areas under the army’s control east of Deir al-Balah.
Gunfire also struck residents' homes along Salah al-Din Street east of Deir al-Balah, causing panic among residents. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
Israeli artillery shelling also hit areas northeast of the Bureij refugee camp in the central Gaza Strip, while an Israeli drone dropped an explosive device on a tent. No injuries were reported.
Israeli violations of the October 2025 ceasefire have killed at least 1,498 Palestinians and injured 5,306 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, the Israeli genocide killed over 74,000 Palestinians and injured 175,000 in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave's infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, Israeli occupiers set fire to a prayer room and a car and scrawled racist slogans in the town of Mukhmas, northeast of occupied Jerusalem, early Wednesday, according to a local official.
Mohammed Kanaan, a member of Mukhmas' municipal council, told AA that a group of Israeli occupiers attacked the area at around 2 a.m. local time (11 p.m. GMT Tuesday) and set fire to the prayer room and a car.
The occupiers also scrawled racist slogans at the site, Kanaan said, adding that local residents promptly notified the relevant authorities and requested the intervention of firefighting crews to extinguish the blaze.
The attack comes amid ongoing violence by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
It also coincides with the olive harvest season, during which attacks against Palestinian farmers have intensified.
On Monday, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it had documented 136 attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers linked to the olive harvest since the beginning of October.
According to the commission, the attacks included beatings, expulsions, intimidation, gunfire, tear gas, arrests, theft of olives and harvesting equipment, and damage to trees. The incidents have harmed Palestinian farmers and restricted their access to their land.
Israeli army raids and attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel's war on Gaza in October 2023.

articles.title: Latest poll puts Eisenkot ahead of Netanyahu in Israel PM race
articles.summary: A poll published Sunday showed former army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot is leading Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 43% to 38% in suitability for office, while Netanyahu's bloc re...
articles.full_text:
A poll published Sunday showed former army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot is leading Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 43% to 38% in suitability for office, while Netanyahu's bloc remained short of a parliamentary majority.
The survey, released by the Israeli public broadcaster KAN, projected 22 seats for Eisenkot's Yashar party in the 120-member Knesset compared with 20 for Netanyahu's Likud, down one seat from the previous week's poll, ahead of elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
Netanyahu's bloc gained two seats to reach 53, leaving it eight short of the 61-seat majority required to form a government.
Eisenkot's bloc was projected to secure 50 seats, with the remaining 17 going to parties classified by the poll as outside both camps.
Arab parties were projected to win a combined 13 seats, including eight for the Joint List and five for the United Arab List, known as Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas.
Within Netanyahu's bloc, the poll gave nine seats to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party, eight to United Torah Judaism and seven to Shas. The Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance was projected to secure five seats.
Amcha Yisrael, led by former brigadier general Ofer Winter, was projected to win four seats, clearing the electoral threshold after failing to do so in the previous poll.
The survey also indicated substantial voter uncertainty, with 30% of respondents saying they had yet to decide which party to support and 21% saying they were considering not voting.
Meanwhile, 54% supported a televised debate between Netanyahu and Eisenkot before the election, including 38% of respondents who intended to vote for Likud.
The results suggest that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition bloc would secure enough seats to form a government on its own.

articles.title: Türkiye's UN envoy calls on Israel to stop reckless attacks in Syria
articles.summary: Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yıldız called on Israel to end its "reckless acts” in Syria and fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. "...
articles.full_text:
Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yıldız called on Israel to end its "reckless acts” in Syria and fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
"Lasting stability is essential for Syria to rebuild its economy, attract investment, and participate in regional energy and connectivity projects,” Yıldız told a session of the U.N. Security Council on Monday.
"Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity undermine these prospects and show disregard for international law,” he said.
"The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” he added.
Yıldız said Israel’s recent resumption of activities along the so-called "Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra was a further attempt to undermine the 1974 agreement and impose a fait accompli on the ground. "These reckless acts must stop,” he said.
He urged Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497, and to withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. "A stable, sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders, defeating terrorist organizations and contributing to regional peace and economic cooperation serves the interests of all, including Israel,” he added.
"The dissolution of the so-called SDF has opened a new chapter in the integration process,” Yıldız said. "Remaining arrangements should be finalized and fully implemented without delay, in a manner that reinforces Syria’s sovereignty, unity and social cohesion,” he added.
Yıldız described the fight against terrorism as "a critical priority” and welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the global coalition for the enduring defeat of Daesh. "Security and economic recovery must advance hand in hand,” he said.
On refugees, Yıldız said the number of Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye once exceeded 4 million and now stands at around 2.2 million.
He said returns have been gradual because of economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions. Since Bashar Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions. Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.
Addressing the same session, Syria’s U.N. representative Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security "should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”
"They should know very well that there is only one path towards security, which is international legitimacy and the resolutions of the (U.N. Security) Council,” the envoy said.
"Every time they open fire on Syria, they are, as the world has witnessed, at the same time opening fire on itself locally and internationally,” he added. Olabi also urged support for economic recovery, investment, job creation and reconstruction. He called for help rehabilitating schools, hospitals and water and electricity networks and for resources and expertise to clear mines and other remnants of war.

articles.title: Gaza rejects truck taxes, urges Israel to allow 600 daily deliveries
articles.summary: Gaza's Government Media Office on Thursday rejected allegations that it imposes taxes or fees on commercial trucks entering the enclave, accusing Israel of using the claims to just...
articles.full_text:
Gaza's Government Media Office on Thursday rejected allegations that it imposes taxes or fees on commercial trucks entering the enclave, accusing Israel of using the claims to justify restrictions on goods and calling for the daily entry of 600 trucks.
It came in response to allegations made Wednesday by Yoram Halevi, the Israeli government’s coordinator of activities in the Palestinian territories, regarding the imposition of financial charges on traders and measures regulating cash transactions in Gaza.
The media office accused Israel of waging a "disinformation campaign” and attempting to hold Gaza’s government authorities responsible for delays in allowing trucks to enter the enclave.
It said it sent messages to mediators and international bodies to clarify its position and warn against additional Israeli measures that could worsen the humanitarian crisis.
The media office stressed that "no government taxes or fees have been imposed on commercial trucks,” and that it had collected no taxes or fees on commercial activities in the last three years, given the enclave's exceptional humanitarian and economic conditions.
Halevi alleged in a letter to international officials that the Palestinian resistance group, Hamas, was demanding traders pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) for each truck entering Gaza, claiming that it had prompted the private sector to halt coordination for the entry of goods.
The media office said the amount was linked to a "voluntary community initiative” involving businesspeople, public figures, institutions and companies. It said the funds were allocated to support orphans, widows, children and students in need, as well as housing, sanitation and relief projects.
Halevi also alleged that Hamas was requiring traders to sell 30% of their goods in cash to control funds.
The media office said the 30% cash-transaction measures were introduced to address a severe cash shortage, the widespread circulation of worn-out banknotes, and the need to facilitate buying and selling.
It stressed that the Chamber of Commerce initiated the measures and agreed to them, rather than the government deciding unilaterally.
The media office said the "most urgent and highest priority is to ensure the regular and sufficient flow of goods into the Gaza Strip.”
It added that announced understandings, including those reached through the Sharm el-Sheikh track, required Israel to allow aid and supplies into Gaza, specifically 600 trucks daily.
The media office urged mediators, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the U.N. and international bodies to pressure Israel to honor its commitments and verify the facts through direct communication with authorities in the enclave.

articles.title: Netanyahu targets soldiers who testified in ‘NAZA’ documentary
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in t...
articles.full_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary "NAZA" about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing "serious information security offenses and criminal defamation” and causing harm to "Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military operations during its genocidal war in Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a "false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
"There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as "vile” and accusing them of "treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Offir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained "substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was "rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war in Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorizing strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the U.N.’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

articles.title: China, Russia have 'too much to lose' by enabling Tehran: Trump
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Monday he does not believe China and Russia are helping Iran, stating that Moscow and Beijing have "too much to lose" by enabling Tehran. Trump ⁠said on...
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump said Monday he does not believe China and Russia are helping Iran, stating that Moscow and Beijing have "too much to lose" by enabling Tehran.
Trump said on Truth Social that he had seen comments from his critics and opponents that China and Russia were helping Iran.
"If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote.
Trump said in July he trusted China and Russia not to help Tehran in the Iran war, but warned that if they did get involved "it would be very bad for them."
The United States and Iran have been at war since Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host U.S. bases. U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have since killed thousands and displaced millions.
Trump has previously described Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as "neutral" during the Iran war.
Moscow and Beijing maintain close ties with Tehran. Russia has said the Iran war could lead to a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Beijing has condemned Washington's attacks on Tehran as a brazen violation of Iran's sovereignty.
Last month, Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran when the Chinese leader visited Washington and received assurances that China would not do so, the U.S. ambassador to China said at the time.
The warning came amid reports that China had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.
In September, Trump brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three U.S. troops there in July.

articles.title: PM Carney urges Canadian unity ahead of Alberta secession vote
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a push for national unity in oil-rich Alberta on Thursday as the province prepared to vote on whether to pursue a binding referendum on ind...
articles.full_text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a push for national unity in oil-rich Alberta on Thursday as the province prepared to vote on whether to pursue a binding referendum on independence from Canada.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada, but Carney, who grew up in the western province, said: "polls don't vote."
"We need people to show up and vote and stand up for Alberta, stand up for Canada," he said during a television interview in Calgary.
Speaking later with local business leaders, Carney said he couldn't think of a "worse time to have a referendum," citing a "more dangerously divided world" and friction with the United States.
Alberta's right-wing Premier Danielle Smith says she is against independence but called Monday's non-binding vote to settle a divisive issue.
If a majority votes for independence, she has committed to launching a legally binding separation process. If a majority votes to stay, Smith says she won't approve another referendum.
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP his side might "actually win this referendum."
"I would be very surprised if we got less than 40%," he said in an interview on Tuesday.
Carney has put Alberta's oil industry at the center of his plans to solidify Canada's economy and reduce dependence on the United States, warning close economic ties have been permanently fractured by President Donald Trump.
Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.
Carney has repeatedly cited the proposed pipeline to argue for Alberta's future prosperity within a united Canada.
Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalized fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.
Smith told the CBC that Alberta separatists stepped up mobilization because Trudeau, who left office last year, was "actively trying to kill" the oil industry.
Oil's dominance in separatist discussion makes Alberta "mostly an outlier," said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global secessionist groups.
Secessionist movements regularly have "economic motivations," but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.
"There's no magic line" dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta's case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.
Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, U.S. interests "don't play any role" in Alberta "until we win and become government," at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.
"There's no animosity towards America here," he said. "I can't see why we wouldn't want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world."
Asked about alleged foreign interference on Thursday, Carney said: "our expectation is – to be absolutely clear on foreign governments, United States included – we don't get ourselves involved in their elections, they don't get themselves involved in our elections."

articles.title: Ukraine bins 'energy cease-fire' with attacks on Russian refineries
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared the end of a brief, unreciprocated truce amid g...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared the end of a brief, unreciprocated truce amid growing rift with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the cease-fire, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on Russian refineries. It wasn't possible to independently verify each side's claims.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for Ukrainian defenses and attack operations.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We’re done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4 1/2 years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy cease-fire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy was due in Brussels for talks with European Union leaders attending a summit.
He was traveling to Belgium after visiting London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: "We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender."
"Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine," Kallas told reporters at the summit, which Zelenskyy is scheduled to attend on Friday.
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.
"It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security," he added.
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

articles.title: NYC moves to ban Central Park horse carriages after 150 years
articles.summary: New York City lawmakers are preparing to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, potentially ending a 150-year tourism tradition amid longstanding animal welfare concerns and...
articles.full_text:
New York City lawmakers are preparing to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, potentially ending a 150-year tourism tradition amid longstanding animal welfare concerns and renewed scrutiny following the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.
A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
"The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.
The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.
"We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. "Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”
For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.
"The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.
Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in "The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in "Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
"Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.
Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has "no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin "used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”
"This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.
The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a "humane manner.”
"I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.
The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.
Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

Eight U.S. states, including Iowa and Kansas, announced lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing its ChatGPT chatbot of endangering children by allegedly encouraging them to harm themselves or others.

Florida's attorney general was the first to sue OpenAI, bringing a lawsuit over similar claims in June. The company is also facing dozens of lawsuits alleging ChatGPT aided in mass shootings or other violence.

articles.title: Zelenskyy feels 'betrayed' by Trump over Russia diesel deal
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday he felt betrayed by U.S. President Donald Trump over Washington's diesel supply deal with Russia, warning that shifting U.S....
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday he felt betrayed by U.S. President Donald Trump over Washington's diesel supply deal with Russia, warning that shifting U.S. support and disruptions to battlefield communications could cost Ukrainian lives.
Speaking during a visit to London, Zelenskyy expressed frustration over Trump's recent moves toward Moscow, including an energy cease-fire announcement and criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked by British journalist Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed by Trump, Zelenskyy replied, "Really, yes," but acknowledged that the situation was more complicated than his personal feelings.
"That's why it's painful when President Trump chooses one side ... not our side," Zelenskyy said in an interview on Morgan's "Uncensored" YouTube channel.
He also questioned the advice Trump was receiving, saying the U.S. president was being pushed toward decisions that were not on the right side of history.
Despite the growing tensions, Zelenskyy stressed that Kyiv remained committed to maintaining its partnership with Washington.
"We count on (our) partnership with the United States," Zelenskyy told British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during their meeting at Downing Street.
"We just want to be very honest, very clear, be strong partners," he added.
Trump recently announced an agreement to purchase diesel from heavily sanctioned Russia, alongside an energy cease-fire initiative that caught both Moscow and Kyiv off guard amid the nearly five-year war.
The U.S. president has also criticized Zelenskyy over Ukraine's long-range attacks on Russian energy facilities and suggested that the Ukrainian leader should be replaced.
Intelligence, Starlink concerns
The diplomatic tensions have been compounded by Ukrainian concerns over U.S. intelligence sharing and disruptions to Starlink satellite internet services used by Kyiv's military.
A senior Ukrainian official confirmed that Washington had recently threatened to suspend intelligence on incoming Russian missile launches, information critical to Ukraine's air defenses.
Trump denied the allegation Tuesday.
Ukrainian defense officials also raised concerns that Washington could be behind reduced speeds on some Starlink terminals, which Ukrainian forces rely on to coordinate battlefield operations, conduct strikes in Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy appealed directly to billionaire Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore full service.
"Of course people will die," Zelenskyy said when asked about the potential consequences of the disruptions.
"It's a big mistake," he added, warning that the decision could result in significant loss of life.
However, Zelenskyy acknowledged that the problems might stem from a technical failure rather than a deliberate restriction.
"I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on," he said.
UK pledges support, seeks to ease tensions
Zelenskyy's visit to London included a meeting with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace, followed by a ceremonial honor guard and talks with Burnham at Downing Street.
The British prime minister welcomed Zelenskyy with an embrace and pledged to accelerate deliveries of lightweight multirole missiles used by Ukrainian forces to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
Burnham also said his government was preparing additional sanctions against Moscow.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told the Ukrainian president.
During their meeting, Zelenskyy referred to the latest Russian attacks on Ukraine and acknowledged the difficulties Kyiv was facing in its relationship with Washington.
"We had massive attacks today and it is a pity we had also some difficulties," he said.
Earlier Wednesday, Burnham told Parliament that he intended to help restore relations between Trump and Zelenskyy to ensure continued U.S. support for Ukraine.
He said he would seek to "repair bridges" between the two leaders while avoiding actions that could further strain diplomatic ties.
"I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play," Burnham said.

articles.title: Mexico to require digital platforms to shield minors from harmful content
articles.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday she would sign a decree requiring social media and streaming platforms to protect children and teenagers from violent, sexual and...
articles.full_text:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday she would sign a decree requiring social media and streaming platforms to protect children and teenagers from violent, sexual and other potentially harmful content.
The decree, which will step up scrutiny of big technology companies in Latin America's second-largest economy, comes after an attack by two 18-year-old former students on a high school in the northern state of Coahuila in early October left one person dead and wounded three others.
Digital platforms will have one month to come into compliance with the decree, government adviser Luisa Maria Alcalde said.
Sheinbaum added that if companies failed to follow the decree, the government would back a bill to punish platforms.
Officials said they had already met with representatives of Meta, Microsoft, Apple, TikTok, Google, X and Huawei to discuss the matter. Those companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Mexico's move follows a broader global push to protect minors online, with governments in Europe and Australia tightening oversight of digital platforms and US states pursuing a range of child-safety measures.
Brazil has also moved to strengthen protections for children online. Such measures have raised questions over how to protect minors while safeguarding privacy and freedom of expression.

articles.title: 5 arrested in Norway over suspected NATO procurement fraud
articles.summary: Norwegian police arrested five people Wednesday as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving NATO procurement contracts, with authorities es...
articles.full_text:
Norwegian police arrested five people Wednesday as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving NATO procurement contracts, with authorities estimating losses of at least 1 million euros ($1.1 million).
The suspects were detained in the western Norwegian region of Bergen over allegations that a company and its subcontractors inflated invoices for services provided to NATO vessels visiting ports in northwestern Europe between 2021 and 2025.
Norway's national economic crime unit said the alleged overbilling targeted the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which provides procurement and logistical support to the alliance's 32 member states and their partners.
The investigation also prompted coordinated searches in Germany and Romania, according to Eurojust, the European Union's agency for criminal justice cooperation.
Investigators suspect that the company submitted fraudulent invoices for shore-based services supporting vessels and their crews during port visits. The company is also accused of using an intermediary to bribe public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in contracts involving the NSPA.
Eurojust estimated that NATO member states suffered losses of approximately 1 million euros, although investigators have yet to determine the full financial impact of the alleged scheme.
Authorities searched the company's premises and several residences in Romania, while German investigators conducted raids at two businesses and a private residence.
The company at the center of the investigation has not been publicly identified.
Marianne Bender, a senior public prosecutor at Norway's economic crime unit, warned that rising global defense spending could create greater opportunities for financial misconduct.
"Defence sector budgets are increasing worldwide, which entails an increased risk of economic crime. This is an area we are monitoring closely," Bender said.
"If NATO has been defrauded, there will be a tough crackdown," she added.
The NSPA coordinates purchases of defense equipment, security systems and logistical services for NATO members and partner countries. The alliance itself does not own military assets such as ships, tanks or weapons.

articles.title: France student protests trigger copycat demos in Albania, Greece
articles.summary: Escalating student grievances over housing shortages, high educational costs and diminishing career prospects have erupted into violent clashes in Albania and set off tent encampme...
articles.full_text:
Escalating student grievances over housing shortages, high educational costs and diminishing career prospects have erupted into violent clashes in Albania and set off tent encampments in Greece, reflecting broader European youth discontent amid a regional cost-of-living crisis.
In Tirana, a peaceful demonstration outside the Education Ministry turned violent, leaving 13 people injured, including six police officers, media outlets reported Wednesday.
Police detained 40 people following clashes across the city center, where demonstrators damaged storefronts, targeted banks, and stormed the municipal administration building.
Security forces deployed water cannons, tear gas, and batons to disperse crowds throwing bricks and stone slabs. Albanian media outlet euronews.al reported that five officers were suspended following allegations of disproportionate force and attacks against uninvolved bystanders.
The student movement in Albania has aligned with the broader "Flamingo Revolution" protests, which began as an opposition movement against a luxury real estate development on the Adriatic coast involving Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
The project, backed by Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama, transformed local flamingos into an anti-corruption symbol against the political establishment. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Rama, who has governed since 2013, amid allegations of systemic corruption shared by both the ruling Socialists and opposition Democrats.
Meanwhile, in neighboring Greece, scores of university students pitched tents in central Athens' Syntagma Square facing Parliament Tuesday, defying heavy rain to demand emergency relief from soaring accommodation costs.
Greek students organized a overnight camp-out and concert to press the conservative government for rent caps, increased housing subsidies, and the construction of new state-run dormitories.
Rent for small apartments has surged across Greece, where flat-sharing is uncommon, putting students in direct competition for limited housing with young couples, single-parent households and digital nomads.
The unrest mirrors recent student demonstrations in France, where high school students organized nationwide strikes and blockades over educational underfunding and living costs.

articles.title: French students keep blocking some schools ahead of govt talks
articles.summary: Nearly 200 French high schools were expected to remain closed Wednesday due to ongoing student blockades, as the government promised to improve university admissions. Education Min...
articles.full_text:
Nearly 200 French high schools were expected to remain closed Wednesday due to ongoing student blockades, as the government promised to improve university admissions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told French broadcaster BFMTV that "96% of high schools are open," with no disruptions reported in three-quarters of the country's departments, a day after the fifth round of nationwide protests.
Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher and the Balzac school complex. Balzac's administration suspended in-person classes, citing access difficulties and safety concerns.
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France's university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October.
He expressed openness "to adjustments, possibly substantial ones," while questioning what would replace the platform if it were abolished.
According to Geffray, fewer than 20% of the 90,000 contributions submitted to a government platform collecting students' complaints concerned Parcoursup.
He ruled out immediate changes to the baccalaureate, France's school-leaving examination.
"I'm not going to change the baccalaureate six months before a presidential election; we need to stop constantly reforming," he said.
Student representatives are scheduled to meet Geffray and Baptiste Thursday afternoon as they press for 10 billion euros ($11 billion) in investment.
Pierre Sourzat, president of the organization Les Lyceens!, told Franceinfo that students expected concrete measures after receiving "only crumbs."
Although organizers have not called for a sixth round of protests Thursday, the Union of High School Students urged demonstrators to maintain blockades.
Union President Ryad Rani and other student representatives also called for participation in a "yellow vest" demonstration scheduled for Saturday.
Meanwhile, classes resumed at Kleber High School in Strasbourg, where clashes between students and police had occurred in recent weeks.

articles.title: Indonesia wildfires choke Singapore, force East Timor schools shut
articles.summary: Air pollution in parts of Singapore reached "very high" levels Wednesday while East Timor closed schools, as haze from Indonesian forest fires triggered a regional crisis. The blaz...
articles.full_text:
Air pollution in parts of Singapore reached "very high" levels Wednesday while East Timor closed schools, as haze from Indonesian forest fires triggered a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit "very high" – the country's top level – the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization's recommended average annual exposure of 5 micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary "as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions", the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use "respiratory protection" if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore's National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
"It's a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside," a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
"With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier," the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother – also masked – for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
"Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated ... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler," Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland and when the wind shifted, the flames moved toward their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
"My house is gone," Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
"There's nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn't have the time to grab anything," said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body ASEAN and on Tuesday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Rahman urged a "diplomatic protest."
"We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but ASEAN. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region," he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy labels latest Russian attacks as disrespect toward US
articles.summary: Ukraine accused Russia on Wednesday of violating Donald Trump’s "energy cease-fire" and wasting an opportunity for de-escalation, following a wave of deadly strikes that targeted p...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine accused Russia on Wednesday of violating Donald Trump’s "energy cease-fire" and wasting an opportunity for de-escalation, following a wave of deadly strikes that targeted power supplies nationwide.
Kyiv in particular faced a barrage of powerful ballistic missiles and attack drones targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure, despite the U.S. president's surprise weekend announcement.
Four people were killed in the city and power to at least 600,000 people was cut after significant damage was reported to power facilities and equipment.
Power plants also came under ballistic missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, hitting electricity and heating infrastructure, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted the latest attack as "entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," adding: "Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," he wrote on X.
Trump blindsided both Kyiv and Moscow Sunday by unilaterally announcing an "energy cease-fire," two days after enraging Ukraine's Western allies with news of a deal with heavily sanctioned Russia to supply diesel fuel.
The U.S. leader has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy – and even said he should be replaced as president – for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
A senior Ukrainian official confirmed to AFP reports in recent days that Washington threatened to pull intelligence-sharing with Kyiv that it relies on to detect incoming attacks.
The renewed signs of strain with Trump have cast doubt on those arrangements, as air raid sirens warning of approaching drones or missiles failed to sound on Monday night and Tuesday night before explosions were heard.
That has occurred only rarely in the past. Ukrainian officials attributed the issue to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues.
But Zelenskyy on Tuesday evening said Ukraine had received "no early warning from our partners" about ballistic missile launches, calling it "absolutely unjust."
An aide to Zelenskyy meanwhile said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals also appeared to have been restricted overnight, disrupting "a number of missions" by Ukrainian defense forces.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," said Sergiy Beskrestnov.
A senior Ukrainian official told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that Starlink speeds had been "throttled," suggesting that it was done to Russia's advantage.
"What is important is that this has been ongoing since last night. Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening, so, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning's Russian ballistic attack," they added.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to hold off from striking Russian energy infrastructure, but accused the Kremlin of having "squandered the opportunity for de-escalation" in the nearly five-year conflict.
Russia has previously targeted Ukraine's power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
Ukraine has been pushing its allies for more military support as Kyiv increasingly comes under attack, particularly the supply of advanced interceptor systems to shoot down missiles and fast, jet-powered drones.
Russian ballistic missile attacks were also reported in the eastern region of Kharkiv and Zhytomyr in the northwest, and other strikes hit Sumy in the northeast and Chernigiv in the north.
Two people were killed in the central Dnipropetrovsk region and a further person in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast, the authorities said.
The governor of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, citing preliminary estimates, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defense forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying toward the Russian capital overnight.
Russian authorities said around 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.

articles.title: Air India flight diverted after pilot sends hijack code amid bomb threat
articles.summary: An Air India flight from Frankfurt to New Delhi was diverted to Jaipur Wednesday after the pilot reportedly activated a hijack emergency code following an alleged bomb threat, acco...
articles.full_text:
An Air India flight from Frankfurt to New Delhi was diverted to Jaipur Wednesday after the pilot reportedly activated a hijack emergency code following an alleged bomb threat, according to local media reports.
India Today reported that the mid-air scare occurred when pilots of the Air India flight broadcast a “squawk 7500” emergency signal, the international code for a hijacking.
The alert, first received by Ahmedabad Air Traffic Control, prompted immediate security protocols. The aircraft was rerouted to Jaipur International Airport, where it landed safely. All passengers were deboarded without incident.
Aviation authorities conducted a thorough inspection of the plane after landing. India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation has launched an investigation to determine the circumstances that led the crew to activate the hijack alert.
No explosives were found aboard the aircraft, and authorities have not reported any injuries or further threats. The incident remains under official review.

articles.title: India jails 'Cockroach' leaders for 5 days over protest ban violation
articles.summary: Two leaders of India’s "Cockroach” youth movement were sentenced by a local court to serve five days in jail after being detained during a protest demanding the resignation of the...
articles.full_text:
Two leaders of India’s "Cockroach” youth movement were sentenced by a local court to serve five days in jail after being detained during a protest demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief, the group said Wednesday.
Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among about a dozen people detained by police Tuesday after they climbed over barricades to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar, a historic observatory in central New Delhi that has long been a site for protests.
Police said this week that the site was no longer an official protest venue and accused Das and Ranka of trespassing and defying prohibitory orders.
The arrests follow a sweeping police crackdown over the weekend aimed at preventing mostly young Indians from gathering in New Delhi to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Police briefly detained thousands of demonstrators.
"Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it,” opposition leader Rahul Gandhi wrote on X in a post condemning the arrests as "an act of cowardice.”
Protests have intensified over an ongoing nationwide revision of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated and could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters.
The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
Abhijeet Dipke, the "Cockroach” movement’s founder, criticized Modi in a post on X.
"If you’re so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics,” Dipke wrote.
The "Cockroach” movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience.
Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV undergoes successful lung surgery, Vatican says
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery in Rome on Tuesday, with doctors confirming that the lower lobe of his right lung was removed followi...
articles.full_text:
Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery in Rome on Tuesday, with doctors confirming that the lower lobe of his right lung was removed following the discovery of a malignant tumor.
The 71-year-old Leo returned to his room after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman, who promised further information at a later time. He had a scheduled operation to remove a nodule from his lung on Tuesday, which the Vatican said had gone smoothly.
Subsequent examination confirmed that the nodule was an adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, the Gemelli medical team said.
The pope had announced his planned surgery on Sunday, saying the nodule had been detected during checks at a "very early stage" and was "well localized."
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here,” said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is "excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation,” said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope’s care but knows the team at Gemelli.
But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Spaggiari said he expected the team at Gemelli would perform a biopsy to determine whether Leo has lung cancer followed by the removal of a section or lobe of the lung where the nodule is located.
Both could be done using robotic techniques, and could be performed consecutively, under the same anesthesia, with different specialist teams, Spaggiari said.
A sophisticated robotic bronchoscopy technology called ION allows a biopsy on nodules as small as 3 millimeters (1/10 inch), Spaggiari said. Both the Gemelli and the EIO have the technology, which has been available in Italy for just two years.
Gemelli also has robotic surgical technology, allowing the operation to remove the nodule to proceed "using a minimally invasive technique,” he said.
The technique involves the surgeon making four small incisions in the chest through which the instruments of the so-called da Vinci robot are inserted, he said. The surgeon then controls the robotic arms looking at a screen providing high-definition, 3D views of the surgical site.
"It’s a very well-established technology. This is something we have been doing for 20 years,” he said.
It wasn't known for certain what technique would be used on Leo. Gemelli has documented using both robotic procedures to diagnose and operate in under four hours.
The biopsy risk is "virtually zero,” while the surgical risk is very small, carrying a 0.6% to 0.8% mortality rate for patients in otherwise good health with good heart and lung function, Spaggiari said.
During the surgery, doctors would also remove lymph nodes that drain the segment or lobe. "If all those lymph nodes turn out to be negative, so stage one, then the outlook is very good,” he said, adding that no other treatment would be necessary.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said.
"I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic - a lung nodule, possibly a tumor. He might call it something else; we call it luck,” he said.
EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery - which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome - a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for "Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the "horrible” pain of the fever. "I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
"Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here - the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan.

articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins French student protests amid police clashes
articles.summary: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined French high school students protesting poor learning conditions Tuesday, as largely peaceful demonstrations were disrupted by clashes with po...
articles.full_text:
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined French high school students protesting poor learning conditions Tuesday, as largely peaceful demonstrations were disrupted by clashes with police, who used tear gas to disperse crowds amid reports of thrown projectiles.
Four weeks into nationwide protests over teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and dilapidated school buildings, more than 161,000 people took to the streets of major cities, according to interior ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.
The government has pledged to address the protesters' grievances, but with public finances already strained and borrowing costs at decades-high levels, it has limited options to invest in public services despite pressure from the streets.
The day started with pupils clustered outside schools with placards and megaphones. In Saint-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris, Thunberg joined one of the gatherings.
"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.
"Whether it's not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises ... it's about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future."
In front of Paris City Hall, a youth orchestra played Antonin Dvorak's "New World Symphony." Some musicians had protest stickers on their cellos and violins.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed, down from 800 on a similar protest day a week ago. It said 94.2% of high schools were open.
Six months out from a presidential election that polls suggest could usher in the first far-right government since World War Two, the youth protests, which have been supported by the left, have added to a sense of uncertainty and polarisation.
While most demonstrators marched peacefully on Tuesday, riot police charged and fired tear gas in locations in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalised property and hurled objects at police.
In central Paris, at least one car was set on fire during running confrontations between police and protesters down a central, tree-lined avenue.
In Lyon, the local authorities asked organisers to call off a march after a group of "hostile individuals" preceding the main procession vandalised shops and a petrol station and clashed with police.
While there was no immediate information on who was involved, it is not uncommon in France for street protests to attract so-called "casseurs", a fringe of rioters who seek to confront police and destroy property.
The protest movement and the police response have elicited polarised responses from leading contenders to replace Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who has a chance of reaching the runoff according to polls, joined one of the marches in Paris, where young protesters chanted his name.
"The police are losing their breath running after young people to beat them up and injure them," he said in a post on X.
"The only ones not losing their breath are the young people bravely protesting," he added, accusing the media of failing to show the extent of police brutality.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the presidential race according to polls, has denounced violence by protesters and called for those who have damaged schools - or their parents if they are minors - to pay for repairs.
The government has already introduced a bill that would allow precisely that. It is going through parliament.

articles.title: Mass rallies across France back students protesting school conditions
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday in solidarity with high school students demanding better learning conditions, intensifying pressure...
articles.full_text:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday in solidarity with high school students demanding better learning conditions, intensifying pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as he approaches the end of his term.
Some 161,500 people turned out, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 it gave for the last nationwide demonstrations on Thursday last week.
Unions helping organize Tuesday's rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000.
The numbers suggested snowballing street opposition to the government just six months before France votes for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
On Saturday, national demonstrations against the spiralling cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents fusing together.
The agitation comes as Macron's centrist government struggles to get a cost-cutting budget through parliament, in the teeth of worsening debt that has spooked the bond market.
Although most of Tuesday's demonstrations were peaceful, violence occurred on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the interior ministry said 41,500 people participated.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Among those taking part in a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis was Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. She said she was there because "our future is being robbed".
University students were prominent in Tuesday's demonstrations, alongside teachers and union leaders.
They were also backed by far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose chief, presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon, was seen among crowds in Paris.
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
"We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week's demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

articles.title: France accuses Musk of online harassment, warns of election meddling
articles.summary: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused billionaire Elon Musk of orchestrating online harassment campaigns against European leaders Tuesday, warning that foreign interfere...
articles.full_text:
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused billionaire Elon Musk of orchestrating online harassment campaigns against European leaders Tuesday, warning that foreign interference could threaten France's 2027 presidential election.
Barrot said foreign actors were exploiting political and social divisions to influence public debate ahead of the April-May vote, raising concerns about coordinated disinformation campaigns targeting European democracies.
Speaking at a conference organized by the Paris-based Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), Barrot warned that opponents of democracy would seek to destabilize France during the election period.
He said foreign actors were exploiting contentious issues, including immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, to fuel polarization and social tensions.
Barrot also accused an unidentified Israeli company of creating fake French social media accounts to influence online discussions surrounding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The minister singled out Musk, the owner of social media platform X, accusing him of conducting widespread online harassment campaigns against European leaders to shape domestic political debates.
He said Musk's activities exploited the platform's ability to rapidly amplify politically charged content.
Barrot's remarks came amid weeks of protests by French high school students over their conditions, which he said had been accompanied by hostile online narratives originating from Russia, China, Iran and supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement.
Trump weighed in on the situation last week, claiming on his Truth Social platform that France was experiencing what he described as uncontrolled mass migration.
Musk subsequently echoed those concerns in a post to his 241.5 million followers on X, describing immigration as a gradual invasion and accusing those supporting it of betraying their countries.
Barrot pledged that France would respond firmly to attempts to influence its domestic affairs.
"We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty," he said.
The warnings come as France prepares for a closely watched presidential election in which far-right politician Marine Le Pen is expected to remain a major political force, although her eligibility to run remains a separate legal question.
Concerns about foreign interference have also intensified elsewhere in Europe.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that Russia had interfered in the United Kingdom's 2016 Brexit referendum, which resulted in the country's decision to leave the European Union.
