articles.title: Trump envoy to Greece asked to resign amid ethics scandal
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, has been asked to step down following a series of ethics allegations, including a bribery scandal, the White House's new press secret...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, has been asked to step down following a series of ethics allegations, including a bribery scandal, the White House's new press secretary said Tuesday.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," Katie Zacharia told reporters in her first briefing to the media.
It wasn't immediately clear if Guilfoyle had resigned.
Guilfoyle's requested departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and President Donald Trump registered his unhappiness with reports about Guilfoyle's alleged conduct Monday.
"Well, we're looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. "We're not happy."
Those comments came a day after The Associated Press, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct and will likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly. But in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services – public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination – that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations," they said.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
But after another report appeared later, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr.

articles.title: Russia in touch with US over Ukraine energy cease-fire: Kremlin
articles.summary: The Kremlin said Tuesday that Russia remains in contact with Washington regarding a potential energy cease-fire in Ukraine mentioned by President Donald Trump last week. In remarks...
articles.full_text:
The Kremlin said Tuesday that Russia remains in contact with Washington regarding a potential energy cease-fire in Ukraine mentioned by President Donald Trump last week.
In remarks to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the topic was discussed during Monday's news conference and that he had nothing to add to that conversation.
"Contacts regarding this matter are ongoing," Peskov said, noting that he does not see a correlation between Russia’s position on Ukraine and a deal – unveiled by Trump Friday following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin – for Moscow to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets.
Peskov described the diesel agreement as a "highly mutually beneficial" aspect of Russian-American cooperation.
"This serves the interests of the United States, the interests of global energy markets and the interests of the Russian Federation; that is why it is happening,” Peskov added, claiming that European countries may attempt to hinder the agreement.
Peskov also said that Russia is a country that offers competitive products on global markets and will continue to do so.
He said Kremlin was unaware of reports that the U.S. would cease intelligence sharing with Kyiv, as well as a U.S.- and European-proposed peace plan for the Ukraine war reported by The Washington Post.
The spokesman also said that it was too early to discuss a compensation mechanism for financial losses suffered by Yandex users as a result of recent Ukrainian attacks against the company’s data centers.
On Sunday, Trump announced on his Truth Social media platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate cease-fire on attacks targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios earlier Sunday that Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
Meanwhile, Peskov said Monday that the Kremlin had no immediate comment on the proposed halt, though contacts with the U.S. concerning the topic were ongoing.

articles.title: Sudan’s anti-war coalition calls for immediate humanitarian truce
articles.summary: Sudanese civilian and political groups opposed to the ongoing civil war has called for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian truce and a Sudanese-led peace process after talks M...
articles.full_text:
Sudanese civilian and political groups opposed to the ongoing civil war has called for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian truce and a Sudanese-led peace process after talks Monday with the African Union’s high-level mediation mechanism in Addis Ababa.
The delegation, which included former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, met the Quintet mechanism at the African Union headquarters Monday to discuss efforts to end the conflict and establish a peace process led and owned by Sudanese people.
Participants included U.N. personal envoy Ramtane Lamamra, African Union envoy Mohamed Ibn Chambas, representatives of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), European Union special representative Annette Weber, and observers from Norway and Germany.
In a statement, the groups said an immediate and unconditional humanitarian truce was a priority to protect civilians, ensure aid delivery and pave the way for peace.
Coalition leader Shehab Ibrahim told Sudan Tribune that the delegation presented a framework based on three parallel tracks: a temporary cease-fire, humanitarian assistance and comprehensive political dialogue.
He said the tracks must proceed simultaneously, warning that addressing them separately would complicate efforts to resolve the conflict.
The groups said political dialogue should address the root causes of the crisis and establish the foundations for an inclusive peace and a sustainable democratic civilian transition.
They called for civilian forces to participate in designing and leading the process under fair criteria to prevent any one party from dominating it. The statement also called for the exclusion of the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement and their affiliated organizations.
Ibrahim said discussions addressed the possible participation of members of the dissolved National Congress Party, which ruled under ousted President Omar al-Bashir.
The coalition outlined its objections to the former ruling party’s inclusion, arguing that dismantling the previous regime’s economic base and safeguarding independent military decision-making remained essential priorities.
The sides agreed to form a joint preparatory committee to set an agenda, determine participants, select venues for future talks and expand engagement with international facilitators.
Discussions also covered future constitutional structures and governance arrangements, which the parties agreed to address in broader political negotiations.
The groups urged regional and international mediators to coordinate their efforts under a unified framework bringing together the Quad, the Quintet and the Troika.
They also called for stronger pressure on the warring parties and those obstructing peace, including extending the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan, halting external support fueling the conflict, cutting off funding for the war and holding those responsible for atrocities accountable.
The statement rejected granting legitimacy to authorities established as a result of the war and stressed the importance of preserving Sudan’s territorial integrity and national unity.
The groups said they would continue engaging with the Quintet, the Quad and other actors seeking a peaceful resolution. They also pledged to broaden support for an independent civilian anti-war movement that does not align with either side.
Their stated goal is to restore Sudanese people’s rights to security, freedom and democratic civilian rule and complete the path of the December Revolution, which led to al-Bashir’s overthrow in April 2019.
Sudan’s war began on April 15, 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces following a power struggle between their leaders. The conflict has displaced millions and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.

German police temporarily closed Nuremberg’s Albrecht Duerer Airport and suspended flights Tuesday following a suspected in-flight emergency on a plane arriving from Greece, authorities said.
"We are operating under the suspicion of an in-flight emergency, though this has not yet been officially confirmed," a police spokesperson said, adding that investigations are ongoing.
The heavy police deployment was triggered shortly before the scheduled landing of a flight from the Greek island of Corfu. According to airport officials, the aircraft landed safely.
The German news agency Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa) reported that an emergency code was squawked while the plane was airborne. German Air Force Eurofighters were subsequently scrambled to escort the aircraft.
Tuesday’s security scare followed a disruption early this morning when three airline pilots independently reported a possible drone sighting near the airfield during takeoffs and landings.
Border police, working with air traffic control and airport management, immediately launched a search involving a police helicopter, but no drone was found.
The incident caused minor delays to six flights – two arrivals and four departures – before normal operations resumed.

articles.title: Sofia calls Moscow envoy over 11 missing in drone attack on ship
articles.summary: Bulgaria summoned Russia’s ambassador Tuesday after 11 sailors went missing when a drone attack sank their ship off the Bulgarian coast, marking the second possible deadly sinking...
articles.full_text:
Bulgaria summoned Russia’s ambassador Tuesday after 11 sailors went missing when a drone attack sank their ship off the Bulgarian coast, marking the second possible deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area within a week.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation."
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incidents.
"This is absolutely unacceptable – another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
The attacks were also condemned by Ukraine and the EU.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. "Those responsible should be held accountable."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X Tuesday that the strike "once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives."
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage," he said.
Speaking with von der Leyen and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte by telephone Tuesday, Radev urged their support to bolster his country's maritime and airspace surveillance, the Bulgarian government said in a statement.
NATO will continue to adjust its military presence on its eastern flank "as needed," Rutte said.
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets.
President Iliana Iotova identified the vessel as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and said a search and rescue operation was ongoing.
Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship – seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis – were rescued and none seriously injured.
A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued.
After meeting Radev in Sofia, Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova said she had no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, the Bulgarian government said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.

articles.title: Moscow, Kyiv hold fire as Trump's energy cease-fire finally unfolds
articles.summary: Donald Trump's "energy cease-fire" finally unfolded Tuesday when Moscow did not hit any Ukrainian energy targets and Kyiv revealed it had not hit Russian refineries for two days. R...
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump's "energy cease-fire" finally unfolded Tuesday when Moscow did not hit any Ukrainian energy targets and Kyiv revealed it had not hit Russian refineries for two days.
Russia's Defense Ministry, in its daily summary of overnight strikes, made no mention of Ukrainian energy facilities. A Kremlin spokesperson, asked about the energy cease-fire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. However, one missile came down just over a kilometer from a plant providing heating to much of the city of Lviv, in the west.
Trump's cease-fire announcement Sunday came two days after his declaration of a deal that lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports to allow Russia to supply almost 2 million metric tons of diesel, a bid to lower U.S. fuel prices.
Reuters and other media outlets have reported that U.S. officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it halts its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had not hit Russian refineries for two days, since Trump announced the cease-fire, but that Russia had continued attacks on energy and critical infrastructure during that time. Russia struck six Ukrainian energy sites Monday.
It was not clear whether Russia had deliberately avoided targeting energy infrastructure overnight into Tuesday.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports – for a sharp rise in U.S. diesel prices this year, a headache for his Republican party ahead of Congressional midterm elections in three weeks.
Most analysts, however, say Trump's war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise.
Four people were killed by Russian strikes in Ukraine's second city, Kharkiv and at least a dozen were injured across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
The Ukrainian air force said it had not received prior surveillance warnings before Russia fired six ballistic missiles at Kyiv late Monday, prompting widespread anxiety in online comments from residents. "The causes are being investigated," it said in a statement.
Intelligence about preparations for ballistic missile attacks has been part of the information that the U.S. provides to Ukraine, Ukrainian officials say.
Zelenskyy's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Tuesday that Kyiv continues to receive intelligence data from the United States.
Speaking at a Warsaw security conference, Sybiha said the U.S. request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine's position had strengthened, alluding to Trump's comment to Zelenskyy in a tense Oval Office meeting last year that "you don't have the cards."
"In less than two years, we have gone from 'having no cards' to 'not playing your cards.' That is an achievement," Sybiha said.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine supports the idea of an energy truce, but he has accused Moscow of violating the cesaefire – which Moscow has not acknowledged signing up to.
"This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy cease-fire, we will respond," Zelenskyy told a security conference in Warsaw on Monday.
The Ukrainian air force said Tuesday that damage had been recorded at 17 locations overnight. Air defense units downed 88 out of 108 Russian drones, it said.
A cargo terminal in the southern Mykolaiv region and transport infrastructure in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region were damaged.
In Kharkiv, four people were killed and at least 11 injured in a residential building. In the western Khmelnytskyi region, a hospital was damaged, regional officials said.

articles.summary: India police arrested Tuesday the leaders of a popular youth movement after they entered a blocked protest site in capital New Delhi, their Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said Tuesday...
articles.full_text:
India police arrested Tuesday the leaders of a popular youth movement after they entered a blocked protest site in capital New Delhi, their Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said Tuesday.
Opposition parties and supporters of the movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a security clampdown to demand the resignation of the head of India's election commission, accusing it of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world's most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Delhi Police said on Monday that Jantar Mantar in the heart of the capital had been taken off the list of designated official protest sites.
The site has been sealed off for several days by yellow metal barricades and guarded by a heavy police presence.
But a video posted online by CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke Tuesday showed protesters clambering over the barricades, running into the empty space and waving the national flag – before police chased and detained them.
"CJP sneaks inside to reclaim Jantar Mantar," the group said in a post on social media, adding that those detained included leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde.
"All of them have been detained by Delhi Police," it added.
Delhi Police had announced three official sites on Monday as alternatives to Jantar Mantar, where protesters have gathered for decades – including CJP demonstrations that led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal in July.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke said, tagging Modi in his post.
Modi, in comments at a business conference in New Delhi on Tuesday, called India the "mother of democracy," but did not refer directly to the protests.
"In our country, people openly debate a wide range of issues and discuss different perspectives," he said.

articles.title: Govts will have to listen to people on Palestine: Husam Zomlot
articles.summary: The Palestinian Ambassador to the U.K. Husam Zomlot has said that pro-Palestinian demonstrations in Britain have continued for three years and that the movement is growing in size,...
articles.full_text:
The Palestinian Ambassador to the U.K. Husam Zomlot has said that pro-Palestinian demonstrations in Britain have continued for three years and that the movement is growing in size, visibility and influence.
Zomlot described the British government's announced sanctions targeting activities linked to Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a significant step, while calling for international solidarity to continue.
Speaking in London over the weekend, Zomlot said tens of thousands of people in Britain had continued to take to the streets in support of Palestine, adding that the movement had become louder, stronger and more effective.
Referring to the British government's announced measures targeting settlement-related economic activity, Zomlot welcomed the move as an important development in the right direction.
He stressed the significance of measures addressing settlement goods, services and activities supporting the expansion of settlements, arguing that governments would ultimately have to respond to public demands.
Drawing a comparison between international solidarity with Palestine and the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa, Zomlot said London had been a major center of the global movement against apartheid.
He argued that London was once again playing an important role in an international movement, this time focused on justice and freedom for Palestine, ending the genocide in Gaza and opposing the occupation.
Zomlot said the growing global movement for Palestinian rights was a source of hope, pointing to London's historical role in the anti-apartheid campaign as a precedent for international solidarity.
Zomlot stressed that support for Palestine extended beyond the United Kingdom, with people around the world continuing to speak out and demand action.
He said sustained public pressure could influence government policies and emphasized the importance of people continuing to make their voices heard.
Zomlot said the growing international movement for justice and freedom for Palestine gave him hope, underlining the importance of maintaining solidarity and public engagement.

At least 19 people were injured, five seriously, when a minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a train on the French side of the Channel Tunnel on Thursday evening, authorities said, adding that no deaths were reported and none of the injuries were life-threatening.
The minibus was transporting truck drivers preparing to board a Le Shuttle train for a journey through the tunnel linking France and Britain.
The driver was among those injured, but none of the injuries were considered life-threatening, according to a statement from the local prefecture.
Emergency crews, including a helicopter-based medical response team and border police, were dispatched to the scene as rescue operations continued.
The incident also disrupted rail services, with two Eurostar trains operating between France and England listed as canceled Thursday evening.
The local deputy prefect was expected to hold a news conference at Eurotunnel's nearby headquarters at 10:30 p.m. local time (8:30 p.m. GMT) to provide further details on the accident.

articles.title: Nvidia, Apple reportedly gave $25 million each for Trump's ballroom
articles.summary: Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for U.S. President Donald Trump's planned White House ​ballroom, according to a report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private d...
articles.full_text:
Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for U.S. President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project.
The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chair of telecommunications company Dish Network, the Washington Post reported.
The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post.
The White House said it would not release information about the donors, which spokesperson Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."
"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," Ingle told Reuters.
Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said.
Apple declined to comment.
The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say it raises questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms.
Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility.
The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term.
The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab.
The U.S. Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful."
The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure.
Trump says a planned 8,360-square-meter (90,000-square-foot) ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

articles.title: Syrian gas pipeline targeted in another sabotage attack
articles.summary: A gas pipeline in Syria's northeast was damaged in a "sabotage attack, " the state-owned petroleum company said Thursday, the latest such incident against an energy conduit in rece...
articles.full_text:
A gas pipeline in Syria's northeast was damaged in a "sabotage attack, " the state-owned petroleum company said Thursday, the latest such incident against an energy conduit in recent weeks.
The explosion followed a separate incident on Thursday morning in which a pipeline transporting oil products from the coastal city of Baniyas to the central province of Homs was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage aimed at stealing fuel.
Years of civil war before the fall of longtime dictator Bashar Assad in late 2024 devastated Syria's oil, gas and electricity sectors, with the country becoming heavily reliant on imports to meet its needs.
"The Al-Jabsa production gas pipeline was targeted" in Hasakah province, causing a fire, the Syrian Petroleum Company said, according to official news agency SANA.
The company said that the 16-inch pipeline exploded at 5:15 p.m. in an area about 60 km from the city of Al-Shaddadi.
Technical teams isolated the damaged section by closing valves at the plant and the Deir ez-Zor gas station in the al-Bughailiya area, while firefighting and safety crews headed to the site to secure the area, the statement said.
"Relevant authorities are monitoring the situation. The area has been cordoned off, the isolation valves on either side of the targeted section have been closed, and the surrounding area has been secured," the company said.
That incident at the Baniyas-Homs oil products pipeline caused a gasoline leak, the company said, adding that work was continuing to repair the damage and restore the line to service.
The state petroleum company said last week that an oil pipeline in the country's northeast was also damaged in a sabotage attack.
On Sept. 29, sabotage targeting a gas pipeline in eastern Syria caused an explosion, according to SANA.
And in early October, an explosion at a gas pipeline near the capital Damascus took three power stations offline.
The incidents come after demonstrations last month over rising fuel prices, which authorities linked to price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

articles.title: China, North Korea open long-delayed bridge to strengthen ties
articles.summary: China and North Korea opened a border bridge Thursday after more than a decade of delays, signaling a further strengthening of ties between the neighboring nations. China's officia...
articles.full_text:
China and North Korea opened a border bridge Thursday after more than a decade of delays, signaling a further strengthening of ties between the neighboring nations.
China's official Xinhua News Agency reported that a ceremony for the launch of the New Yalu River Bridge was held in the morning.
An online video from state media outlet China News Service showed trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea waiting on the bridge, which was also decorated with the flags.
Beijing expected that the four-lane, 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) crossing, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju, would further promote economic, trade and "people-to-people" exchanges.
During the ceremony, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address that the crossing would become a new landmark symbolizing the two nations' traditional friendship, Xinhua reported.
He hoped both sides would seize the opportunity of the opening to continue to enhance connectivity and explore potential for cooperation in border areas, it said.
"The relations between China and North Korea have entered a new stage, embarking on a new chapter," he was quoted as saying.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also made a video address, the report added.
The bridge initially was expected to enter use in 2014, when China had apparently completed construction on its side. But the date came with no opening and without North Korea doing corresponding work on its side.
The absence of substantial work in Sinuiju fueled speculation that Pyongyang was wary of becoming more economically dependent on China or displeased with Beijing voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program. Some observers suggested North Korea and China also differed over the bridge's location.
The setback over the bridge prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the ruling Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city.
Observers said the new bridge would likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually.
It is expected to lessen the burden on an aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. That decades-old bridge carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time.
The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border, which stretches more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles).
The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations. Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.
China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has prioritized Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.
China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea's external trade was with China.

articles.title: Austria students resist school headscarf ban over targeting Muslims
articles.summary: A headscarf ban for girls under 14 has triggered widespread protests across Austria as the new school year begins, with dozens of students refusing to comply in classrooms and on t...
articles.full_text:
A headscarf ban for girls under 14 has triggered widespread protests across Austria as the new school year begins, with dozens of students refusing to comply in classrooms and on the streets.
Austria's conservative-led government has insisted the ban, introduced Sept. 1, promotes gender equality and protects Muslim girls from "segregation and oppression."
But critics argue it disproportionately targets Muslims, infringes upon religious freedom and is forcing young girls to dress in a way that makes them feel uncomfortable.
Since the ban took effect, education authorities across Austria have held 127 meetings with parents and filed 52 reports over alleged breaches of the law, according to the Education Ministry.
Opponents of the ban have also held protests across the country, with several hundred people gathering each time.
At a demonstration in Vienna, Zehra, 37, who did not want to give her last name, said her two daughters, ages 9 and 13, were "sad and angry" about the ban.
"We raise our children by telling them, 'You can decide who you want to be' – and this law is the exact opposite," she said.
Seham, 12, said she felt "afraid" to remove her headscarf at school "because I'd worn it for two years and it felt like a part of me."
After discussions with school leaders, she said she was allowed to cover her hair with an alternative non-traditional head covering, but would still "rather wear the full headscarf."
Roughly 8% of Austria's 9 million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.
They suffer the highest rates of racism and discrimination against Muslims in the European Union, according to a 2024 report by Europe's FRA rights agency.
In the 2024 elections, the far-right Freedom Party won for the first time even though it failed to form a government. The anti-immigration party continues to top voter opinion polls.
The new law is Austria's second attempt to restrict headscarves in schools after a coalition between the conservatives and the Freedom Party introduced a ban for primary school students in 2019.
That law was overturned by the constitutional court on the grounds that a regulation targeting only Muslims was incompatible with religious neutrality.
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria, which is supporting legal action against the new headscarf ban, said it had received about 70 reports from families about difficulties during its implementation.
"A law that was justified as protecting children's welfare is putting precisely those children under pressure at school," the group said in a statement.
The constitutional court confirmed to Agence France-Presse (AFP) that it had received a legal complaint about the law and a decision is expected in the first half of 2027.
When girls refuse to comply with the law, schools are required to hold a series of discussions with students and their parents before cases are referred to education authorities.
Ultimately, parents who continue to ignore the ban can be fined.
In a statement sent to AFP, Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr said the fact there had only been 127 meetings so far showed "that the vast majority of pupils and parents are cooperative."
"In addition, the figures show that the discussions held with the parents concerned in the event of a violation are, for the most part, successful," he added.
Education authorities in Vienna said that "on the basis of the discussions held so far, the impression has emerged that the girls wish to wear the headscarf of their own accord."
Sandy, 12, said she began wearing a headscarf about a year ago because "I place a lot of importance on my religion and I want to be able to live it."
A teacher who has worked with two affected girls in the capital told AFP there was no sign they were being forced to wear headscarves.
The girls had spent weeks adapting to the new rules and searching for acceptable alternatives to headscarves, said the teacher, who wished to remain anonymous. "It is very uncomfortable for them."

articles.title: 32 children, 1 teacher dead in NW Pakistan school roof collapse
articles.summary: A school roof collapse in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar killed 32 pupils and a teacher Thursday, a hospital official said. Twenty more students were taken to hospital...
articles.full_text:
A school roof collapse in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar killed 32 pupils and a teacher Thursday, a hospital official said.
Twenty more students were taken to hospital after the collapse, which authorities blamed on "weak infrastructure." Others in the densely populated neighborhood described a close call.
Resident Sohail told Agence France-Presse (AFP) "everyone began screaming in panic" after his niece managed to find her way home after escaping the building to inform them of the collapse.
"When I arrived at the scene, I saw around 10 to 15 children trapped beneath the rubble, with debris piled up to their necks. We quickly pulled them out," he said.
Asim Khan of Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital said the death toll had risen to 33 by Thursday evening, with most of the victims aged between four and 14.
"A total of 20 injured children were brought to the hospital, most of whom have been discharged. Three severely injured children, who sustained head injuries, have been admitted to the hospital," Khan said.
The injured and deceased included 12 girls and a female teacher, Khan added.
A spokesman for the emergency rescue service in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province said schoolchildren were crushed and trapped after the roof gave way.
"When the Rescue 1122 emergency response teams arrived at the scene, they found that one roof had collapsed onto another, causing the classroom below to be crushed and trapping children inside," spokesman Bilal Ahmad Faizi said.
Dozens of people were at the scene.
Images released by the emergency services showed rescue workers in high-visibility vests scrambling to move debris, rubble and dirt.
A senior Peshawar-based official said that initial reports suggested the roof collapse was due to "weak infrastructure."
"The school owner has been detained," the official said on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to talk to the media.
Bodies wrapped in white cloth were seen being carried out of the hospital as volunteers arrived to help identify the victims.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed "deep sorrow and grief over the loss of precious lives," according to a statement.
"The Prime Minister extends his condolences to the bereaved families and prays for them to have the strength and patience to bear this irreparable loss," the statement said.
President Asif Ali Zardari described the roof collapse as a "heartbreaking tragedy."
Resident Sher Ahmed blamed "substandard construction materials" for the tragedy and called for an investigation.
"With profound grief and sorrow, I urge the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take strict action against anyone found responsible so that such tragedies can be prevented in the future," he said.
Roof and building collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and substandard construction materials in the South Asian nation of more than 240 million people.
In June, more than a dozen children were killed when a roof collapsed at a tutoring center in the eastern city of Lahore.
